title: Be like Sophie Cunningham, not Chris Simms — never give in to the outrage mob
excerpt:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Sophie Cunningham understands something that very few others in the sports world seem to.

You n...
body_text:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Sophie Cunningham understands something that very few others in the sports world seem to.

You never, ever cave to the mob if you haven't done anything wrong.

The Indiana Fever guard proved as much this summer after she came out against biological males competing against females in sports.

Sophie Cunningham No. 8 of the Indiana Fever celebrates after making a three-point shot in the first half against the Minnesota Lynx at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on Sept. 22, 2026, in Indianapolis, Ind. (Getty Images)

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPARKS SOCIAL MEDIA MELTDOWN BY SPEAKING OUT TO PROTECT WOMEN'S SPORTS

Her stance prompted her to garner the title "MAGA Barbie." It sparked fans to boo her when she entered the game in cities such as Seattle. It caused a sports reporter to say that she is "unafraid to be blatantly transphobic" and fans to call for her suspension.

Did Cunningham buckle? Hell no. She doubled down with an Instagram post that declared she isn't backing down for anyone.

This is the only way to do it. If there's one thing the mob hates more than anything, it's courage. You show it to them, they go away. It's just sad that so few seem to possess it.

NBC Sports football analyst Chris Simms was the latest to bow to online outrage over some perfectly reasonable comments. After Oregon quarterback Dante Moore was knocked out of Saturday's game due to a helmet-to-helmet hit by USC's Desman Stephens II, Simms did what an analyst is paid to do: analyze.

At halftime, Simms said that Moore's injury was a "Debbie Downer" moment because fans want to see teams at full strength. He then shared some advice his father told him about how to "make sure you get down in time and don't take any big hits." He added how Moore's late slide put Stephens in a "no-win situation."

Quarterback Dante Moore of the Oregon Ducks runs with the football and slides to avoid a tackle from linebacker Desman Stephens II of the USC Trojans during a game at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Sept. 26, 2026, in Los Angeles, Calif. (ISI Photos via Getty Images)

DAN DAKICH CALLS CHRIS SIMMS' APOLOGY OVER DANTE MOORE SLIDE ANALYSIS 'SOFT A-- BULLS--T'

This is an ex-football player talking football. But apparently all Oregon fans wanted to hear was that this was the dirtiest hit in the history of the sport, so Sunday, Simms took to social media to write "I clearly did not show enough sympathy for the situation. I mishandled the situation and I was wrong. I'm sorry for that."

It seems like we see a new one of these every week. Earlier this month, Texas quarterback Arch Manning laughed at an AI meme of ESPN reporter Holly Rowe getting slapped by Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian. He was shamed into apologizing two days later. In July, Sandy Brondello, coach of the WNBA's Toronto Tempo, wanted a foul to be called on Atlanta's Angel Reese, and could be heard telling refs that Reese was a "protected species."

This is common lingo in Australia — Brondello's home country — where it's meant to express frustration over a player getting special treatment. But Brondello still issued a written apology to Reese, saying "I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that."

And then, of course, there was Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown caving last year after doing the Trump dance after a touchdown in a game vs. Commanders. Said St. Brown: "First of all, if I offended anyone, I do apologize. I did not mean to offend anyone. It was just, we're having fun."

It's hard watching these sports figures shed their dignity with each one of these mea culpas. What they don't understand is that they are losing respect from the public every time they issue one. The outrage mob simply sees them as people who will fold the next time they want to sink their hooks into them. And the folks who would have supported them if they stood strong? They now see a spineless pushover.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This doesn't mean that people should never apologize. During his time in Seattle, Richard Sherman was infamous for his inability to ever take accountability for his wrongdoing. That's also a form of weakness — it's just wearing a different costume.

But to surrender when you've done nothing wrong? It's not noble, it's nauseating.

CHARLES BARKLEY DECLARES WNBA IS 'FOR WOMEN ONLY' AFTER ONGOING TRANSGENDER ATHLETE DEBATE

Charles Barkley says WNBA players dislike Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, blaming a mix of jealousy, race, and sexuality for the hostility. (Getty Images)

People like Cunningham know this. Charles Barkley, too. The Hall of Fame hooper is on record saying trans athletes don't belong in women's sports, and the blowback has been almost nonexistent because everyone knows he is going to hold firm in his position. That's the power of integrity.

The vocal minority shouldn't have the influence that it does. Yet it regularly turns titans of the sports world into mush. Don't be like Chris Simms, who gave into the mob. Be like Cunningham, who decided to stand up to it. Sophie's choice is the only choice.

Matt Calkins is a columnist for Outkick, where he focuses on the overlap between sports and culture. Before joining the Fox team, he spent 11 years as a sports columnist for the Seattle Times, where he extracted a two-word quote from Marshawn Lynch and got a Seahawks draft pick to design his apartment.Matt also served as a sports columnist at the San Diego Union Tribune after working as the Blazers beat writer for the Vancouver Columbian. You can follow him on X at matt_calkins.

title: Dan Wilson announces his own firing as Seattle Mariners manager in rare postgame moment
excerpt:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Seattle Mariners manager Dan Wilson personally broke the news to his team and the media Sunday t...
body_text:
Dan Dakich questions why Chris Simms is apologizing over his remarks on injured Oregon QB Dante Moore.

Seattle Mariners manager Dan Wilson personally broke the news to his team and the media Sunday that he will not return for the 2027 season.

Before Game 162 against the Los Angeles Angels, Wilson held a closed-door meeting to inform players and staff.

Postgame, he stepped to the podium to deliver the news publicly and face questions before front-office executives addressed reporters.

Standard MLB protocol calls for front-office executives to issue a news release or hold a solo news conference while the ousted manager stays out of sight.

Manager Dan Wilson of the Seattle Mariners looks on before the game against the Los Angeles Angels at T-Mobile Park on Sept. 27, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (Getty Images)

A manager taking the microphone to announce his own dismissal is virtually unheard of in modern sports.

"This season has been very difficult, and of course, the results have not been what any of us have expected," Wilson said. "As a result, it's concluded that today is my last day as manager of the Seattle Mariners."

Wilson, a former Mariners catcher who took over as manager in August 2024, acknowledged his deep roots in the organization.

"I'm still processing this with my family, and it's a very difficult day," Wilson said. "We love this city. We love this community and we appreciate the organization for what it has meant to the family since coming here as a player in '94. We feel extremely blessed by all the opportunities we've been afforded."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Expectations were sky-high entering 2026.

Coming off a 2025 AL West title and reaching Game 7 of the ALCS, Seattle fell just one win short of the World Series. Instead, the club collapsed to a 76-86 third-place finish.

The downward spiral was driven by offensive regression among core players, inconsistent starting pitching, a second-half bullpen collapse and some of the worst defensive metrics in Major League Baseball.

Manager Dan Wilson removes pitcher George Kirby during the seventh inning against the Philadelphia Phillies at T-Mobile Park on Aug. 25, 2026, in Seattle, Wash. (Getty Images)

Late-season comments from players highlighted a lack of clubhouse accountability as a core failure. Pressed on whether leadership failed to enforce standards, Wilson faced the criticism directly.

"That's always a necessary component, and I think accountability comes in a lot of different ways," Wilson said. "Obviously, I think you look back, and there's a lot of things that you can point to, and perhaps that's one of them."

When asked if the front office made the final decision, Wilson accepted the reality of sports leadership.

Mariners manager Dan Wilson stands before a game against the Brewers at American Family Field in Milwaukee, Wis., on Aug. 18, 2026. (Getty Images)

"I've been in baseball a while, and this is what happens," Wilson said. "Managers shoulder the blame and shoulder the responsibility. And this is obviously difficult."

RED SOX REMOVE INTERIM TAG FROM MANAGER CHAD TRACY AFTER THE TEAM'S REMARKABLE SUMMER TURNAROUND

Seattle Mariners President of Baseball Operations Jerry Dipoto and General Manager Justin Hollander will return in 2027.

Dipoto noted that "collectively we failed to meet our own expectations" and agreed a leadership change was necessary.

Wilson finishes his tenure as Mariners manager with a 187-171 career record.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot
excerpt:
Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed

Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a vill...
body_text:
Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed

Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a village just outside RAF Fairford in the small hours of Sunday – but the fact they have all been released on bail without immediate charge suggests they are not deemed to pose a serious and violent threat.

In a moment where wider geopolitical tensions mean external threats are perceived to be close, the question of whether Iran had a hand in the alleged plot remains open. Nonetheless, the bailing of the men is a mercifully lower-key development in an investigation that appeared of the utmost gravity.

Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform, had earlier insisted that the Fairford incident “proves my point on Iran” and argued that anybody arriving on small boats should not be allowed to move around in the UK. The latter point was an irrelevant argument, already weakened when police said at lunchtime that all five were UK nationals from London.

Though the five were arrested on suspicion of carrying explosives and involvement in a terror plot, after more than 24 hours of searches, nothing had been discovered that would prompt further police action – perhaps explaining why MI5 had no idea that the men and their vans would turn up a mile from the base with unclear intent.

British officials admitted on Sunday the arrests were not led by intelligence, but rather last-minute warnings on the ground. Counter-terror police said they were first aware of three vehicles travelling to the base at 12.45am on Sunday, while a local farmer phoned 999 at 1.36am after the vans blocked the entrance to her drive.

The next day Trump made a characteristically inflated claim that the US and UK had been monitoring the men for “a long time” and that they had been trying to do “big damage”. Threat levels at Fairford have been at the highest level for several days, apparently backing this up – but UK sources say this was related to wider concerns about threats to US bases, not specific to the site.

RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring.

The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”.

That would give Fairford an obvious value, though it is not clear why anyone from London would feel bold enough to attack a military base, given it would be expected to be protected by armed personnel. Rational plotters probably would not expect to survive, and would at least expect the most serious penalties available under law.

When the suspects’ release was announced, there was no firm information from UK counter-terror police about what explosives were found or whether there was deemed to be viable devices in the vans – the kind of information that would immediately point to the degree of intent in any terror plot. Subsequently, it emerged no explosive material had been found.

Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed.

A year ago, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, said the Security Service had “tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in just the one year”. Two Romanian men were found guilty in July of stabbing the Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraati in the leg in Wimbledon two years earlier in a state-directed attack; he worked for the independent Persian channel Iran International.

Yvette Cooper, then home secretary, sanctioned an IRGC-backed terror group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, in July after it claimed responsibility for a series of attacks in the UK, including the burning of four Jewish community ambulances in March. But while four men have pleaded guilty, evidence in the case has yet to be heard in court, with prosecutors only saying so far there was a “terrorist connection”.

In April police closed and searched part of Kensington Gardens near the Israeli embassy in London after an online video appeared to suggest the building had been targeted by drones containing hazardous substances. On that occasion, nothing was found.

title: Australia news live: Chalmers defends record as RBA’s cash rate decision due; killed police officer Mia Lay remembered
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has defended his economic record on the eve of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of ...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has defended his economic record on the eve of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of 2026, as the Reserve Bank remains concerned about persistent inflation.

The RBA board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.

Speaking on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Chalmers emphasised the factors contributing to inflation, saying that Australia was performing well considering what was going on in the world, particularly in the Middle East.

double quotation markWe have a lot going for us and we’ve got a lot of work to do to make sure that in these difficult global circumstances Australia continues to out-perform the world.

We have a big inflation challenge in our economy. It’s made much worse by decisions taken on the other side of the world.

From an economic point of view this war in Iran has been an absolute disaster for Australian families, because they have been asked to pay a hefty price.

The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the Albanese government to find him and bring him home, Australian Associated Press reports.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian-Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.

But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since September 18, leaving her worried for his safety.

double quotation markMy husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.

The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

Chalmers says Australians understand there are ‘inflationary challenges’ in our economy

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the inflationary challenge in the economy is being made “much worse” by the war in the Middle East.

Chalmers, speaking on Channel 7’s Sunrise this morning ahead of the RBA announcement, said the government has focused on savings and delivering surpluses to get government debt down.

double quotation markBut we know that there’s always more work today. I think people understand, people who might be bracing for an interest rate rise later today. … I think people understand that there are inflationary challenges in our economy.

But when you see what’s happening with global oil prices … obviously, factually, that is one the big drivers of inflation that people are having other deal with right now.

Chalmers said he knows that people are under pressure and that interest rate rises add to that pressure.

double quotation markThat’s why we accept our part, our responsibility for our part in this fight against inflation. … And it also means dealing with these longer term economic challenges.

Mia Lay, the Sydney police officer who was killed in a car crash last week, will be among those mourned at National Police Remembrance Day 2026 in Sydney.

New South Wales’ premier, Chris Minns, governor, Margaret Beazley, and police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, will be among the guests at Sydney’s Domain.

Minns said he felt incredibly gratitude for the service of police officers across the state:

double quotation mark[Police] start a shift not knowing what you are going to face, and we ask these young men and women to put themselves in harm’s way to keep the rest of us safe.

Police and counter-terrorism minister, Yasmin Catley, said:

double quotation markMy thoughts are with the families of Constable Lay, Sergeant [Mark] Bransgrove and everyone else who has lost a loved one in the line of duty. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten.

Lay, 20, had worked as a police officer for just 16 months when she was killed “instantly” in the crash in Redfern on Friday. Sgt Mark Bransgrove, who died in July, served in the police service for 38 years, including 30 years in the Forensic Services Group.

Remembrance events will also be held in Broken Hill, Bourke, Orange, Lithgow, Inverell, Dubbo and Tamworth.

Good morning, and happy Tuesday. It’s Nick Visser here to take over the blog. Let’s get to it.

There were 30 drowning deaths in 2025-2026, the highest number in almost a decade, according to a Royal Life Saving Australia report that Australian Associated Press reports on.

Of them, 14 involved more than one death, often related to boating, driving through floodwater, or people exploring unfamiliar environments, chief executive Justin Scarr said.

double quotation markThe message is to know the swimming skills of all the people in your group.

It is the largest spike in deaths since 2016-2017, when 34 lives were lost.

Over the past decade there have been with 229 deaths, or an average of 23 per year.

In the most recent year, 83% of drowning victims were men, 37% were born overseas and a quarter were aged between 65 and 74.

Nearly one-third of the fatal events were related to boating, while driving through floodwater and swimming were the other leading circumstances.

Besides the RBA decision at 2.30pm, the other big political story of the day is that Larissa Waters is standing down as Greens leader.

She said last night that a kidney disease she has been managing has recently worsened and that she needs to stand down.

Here’s our story from political editor Tom McIlroy:

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has defended his economic record on the eve of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of 2026, as the Reserve Bank remains concerned about persistent inflation.

The RBA board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.

Speaking on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Chalmers emphasised the factors contributing to inflation, saying that Australia was performing well considering what was going on in the world, particularly in the Middle East.

double quotation markWe have a lot going for us and we’ve got a lot of work to do to make sure that in these difficult global circumstances Australia continues to out-perform the world.

We have a big inflation challenge in our economy. It’s made much worse by decisions taken on the other side of the world.

From an economic point of view this war in Iran has been an absolute disaster for Australian families, because they have been asked to pay a hefty price.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

Jim Chalmers has defended his stewardship of the economy ahead of what is widely expected to be the fourth interest rate rise of 2026 as the Reserve Bank tries to bring down persistent inflation. More coming up.

Besides the RBA decision at 2.30pm, the other big political story of the day is that Larissa Waters is standing down as Greens leader. We’ll have reaction as it comes in this morning plus the latest on who might replace her.

title: Lane Kiffin is already somehow blaming the SEC's new conference schedule for LSU's injuries
excerpt:
Will Stein discussed his team's schedule and notes that he'd love to only have to play 8 conference games instead of the mandatory 9.

For years, the SEC has enjoyed a bit of an advantage over other c...
body_text:
Will Stein discussed his team's schedule and notes that he'd love to only have to play 8 conference games instead of the mandatory 9.

For years, the SEC has enjoyed a bit of an advantage over other conferences when it comes to record, rankings, and strength of schedule: they played fewer conference games.

The Pac-12, when that conference existed in its previous form, for example, played nine games against other conference teams. So did the Big Ten. The SEC, however, had just eight. With four non-conference opponents, some schools could choose to schedule four likely wins, before entering SEC play.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

An ideal example is the 2025 Missouri Tigers. Missouri's non-conference slate was Central Arkansas, Kansas, Louisiana, and Massachusetts. Four games in which they'd be overwhelming favorites, four wins secured before conference play started.

FLORIDA GATORS, MISSISSIPPI STATE SOAR, USC TUMBLES IN LATEST INEXPLICABLE AP TOP 25 POLL

Missouri Tigers head coach Eli Drinkwitz reacts during the first half against the Texas A&M Aggies at Faurot Field at Memorial Stadium in Columbia, Missouri. (Jay Biggerstaff/Imagn Images)

Missouri proceeded to win just four conference games, 29-20 over South Carolina, 23-17 over Auburn in double overtime, a 49-27 win over Mississippi State, and 31-17 over Arkansas. But, thanks in large part to their four scheduled wins, the Tigers remained in the AP Poll for most of the season, providing a "ranked" opponent for Texas A&M, Vanderbilt, Alabama, and Oklahoma. They did not beat a team that finished the season with a winning record on their way to finishing 8-4.

Incredibly, with this resume, the Tigers were ranked in 12 of 16 polls during the regular season. And why not? 8-4 doesn't look bad, does it? That's a solid season in a tough conference, if you aren't paying close attention. Now remove one of those scheduled non-conference wins, and suddenly the road to 8-4 looks a lot harder. Which is the point other conferences made when arguing against the SEC's endless complaints about strength of schedule.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Well, for 2026, the SEC finally moved to nine conference games and eliminated the "extra" win many of the member programs used to their advantage. And even through just a few weeks of conference play, new LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin is already using it as an excuse.

LSU head coach Lane Kiffin gestures toward an official during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Mississippi in Oxford, Miss., on Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)

Ahead of last weekend's matchup against Texas A&M, Kiffin complained sarcastically, and inaccurately, about the perceived scheduling issues hurting the Tigers with Marcel

"Obviously we just played the best one in the country last week thinking he can hurt you even when you have the right call on and everybody covered and a guy comes free," he said. "Obviously he (Chambliss) played great a year ago here in the stadium, so this is one of those scheduling quirks just like last week where never in that LSU-Ole Miss series had it ever been played two times in a row."

That was, of course, incorrect, but Kiffin wasn't done there in going after the SEC for its scheduling practices. LSU is dealing with its fair share of injuries through the first few weeks of the season, including to star linebacker Whit Wheeks and tight end Trey'Dez Green.

Per ESPN's Marty Smith, LSU's injuries are a direct result of the SEC's nine-game conference schedule. Which is odd because his team has played just two conference games so far.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Smith posted that Kiffin explained that it's an indication of the differences "versus other conferences, and how (they) don’t have to play players or play them as long."

"Be careful what you wish for, SEC," Kiffin said.

Head Coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers prepares to face the Ole Miss Rebels at Vaught Hemingway Stadium in Oxford, Miss., on Sept. 19, 2026. (University Images via Getty Images)

Ah. Yes. Classic Lane Kiffin. There is no outcome that doesn't have a predetermined excuse. No other schools face injuries. No other games require playing starters. When the SEC had eight conference games, it wasn't an advantage, but with nine, they're at a significant disadvantage. Even when they've only played two conference games so far. One of those games was against a very bad Texas A&M team, where the score was 35-6 in the fourth quarter and the outcome was never in much doubt.

The Tigers shouldn't have much to worry about with powerhouse McNeese State coming into town next weekend either.

Curiously, Kiffin never addresses the impact of travel, rest, and recovery on other conferences. Like, for example, USC, which played a road game in New Jersey, then turned around and played a home game in LA a week later. That's a ~6,000 mile round trip road game. LSU's longest road trip of the season is Lexington, Kentucky. Their entire travel schedule is less than one USC road game. That stuff matters as Kiffin would say if it were impacting his team.

UCLA has road games traveling 8,120 one-way miles. USC is 9,500 miles. Just a few examples. The "woe is me" act Kiffin puts on might be effective for the SEC boosters in friendly media outlets. It's just not backed up by any reality we live in. But it's a near-certainty he'll be running the same playbook after the season to try and get the SEC back to eight conference games. Then he'll find something else to complain about.

title: DR. MARC SIEGEL: What 18 years at Fox taught me about courage and faith
excerpt:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses his book, 'The Angels Among Us,' which shares stories of divine intervention.

I joined Fox in early 2008 as a contributor. I was struck from ...
body_text:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses his book, 'The Angels Among Us,' which shares stories of divine intervention.

I joined Fox in early 2008 as a contributor. I was struck from the beginning by the network's flexibility and creativity, allowing me to expand my role from expertise in infectious diseases to health policy and Obamacare.

I was able to flex various journalistic muscles, too. I was sent to Phoenix to examine Sen. John McCain’s health records but ended up with the opportunity to deliver on-air reports.

I began to report for the network in earnest in 2012, and then in the spring of 2013, during the Boston Marathon, when two self-radicalized brothers executed the largest terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11, I managed to get permission from our top executives to head up there.

DR MARC SIEGEL: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, THE DEADLY HEALTH CRISIS IS STILL CLAIMING LIVES

On the way, I somehow convinced the PR team at Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) to grant me the very first interview with a survivor — a woman. Our excellent production team wasn’t expecting me, as we had our top reporters already in the field, but they quickly transitioned to supporting and guiding me. She had been blown off her feet and badly wounded her leg. Her would-be boyfriend had carried her down one-way streets (going in the opposite direction of the cars) to MGH.

We were ready. She looked straight into the camera and said, "We can’t let the terrorists win. We must stay strong and not be afraid. Boston is a great city."

Ten years later, another top Fox executive sent me to East Palestine, Ohio, following the train wreck there. One of the best field producers in the business came with me, and while I was in the neighborhood doughnut shop sampling the best doughnuts I’d ever had, she was assembling an array of guests who had all been injured or affected by the toxic smoke.

FOX NEWS MEDIA'S SPOTLIGHT AWARDS CELEBRATE BEHIND-THE-SCENES STARS AS NETWORK NEARS 30 YEARS

The ERs in the area were calling it "situational anxiety," but outside the temporary state health facility, I interviewed patients who were having trouble breathing while the smoke in the air gave everyone, myself included, a sore throat. People who swam in the river developed rashes, and the long-term health risks remained unknown.

The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed.

We are a family that has developed strong bonds, and we look out for each other. When my father died earlier this year at age 102, the entire Fox management team, from the CEO on down, came to the funeral.

The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed.

BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES

Senior Correspondent Ben Hall brings out the best in the Fox team, and they inspire him. Chief National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin was crucial to arranging his extraction from Ukraine after a horrific near-death experience when his car was bombed and his cameraman and producer were killed in 2022. He survived, thanks to many angels, messengers from God, as I write in my new book, "THE ANGELS AMONG US."

Here’s what Benjamin Hall shared with me about what he was thinking on the day he and his team were attacked in Ukraine:

"At this moment of trying to stay strong, I think of how I am going to get home. I think of my children. Our car has burned totally to pieces, and we are down on the road, down a slight little dip in the road where we are lying, and this one car comes out of nowhere, and it drives past us. And I am shouting at it, ‘We’re here! We’re here!’ And it doesn’t see us, and it keeps driving. And it is a car of Ukrainian special forces, and this same car, amazingly, has engine trouble ten minutes or so down the road, and they have to stop to figure that out. And because of that, they drive back again!"

Hall believes this event is a sign directly from God.

DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE

"I have pulled myself further up by this time, dragging myself along, up toward the road, and as the car comes back again, I don’t know it’s coming. There it is… The last thing I remember is this guy jumping out. He grabs my body armor, grabs the back of my arm, and pulls me along the ground, running to his car."

Is the vision of his daughter that he sees after the missile hits actually an angel? It’s the question everyone has, and I ask it of Hall.

An image of  Fox News contributor Dr. Marc Siegel's forthcoming book 'The Angels Among Us' (Fox Books)

MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME

"Yeah, 100%, either she is an angel that comes to me when I need her, and she gives me the strength I need, and she brings me back, or it is because my body and my mind are calling for her. It’s after the first and then the second shell, when I go into this other world, that’s when I get shrapnel in the eye, and it takes out part of my skull. So, I am already pretty badly injured at this point. Then the third shell takes off my leg, my foot. But I’ve no doubt that my daughter is sent to me, and either it is God who sends her or my body needs it, and my mind goes to the place it has to go to find the right strength."

Ben Hall’s father had recently died in 2022, and Hall had just buried him when he flew from his father’s funeral straight to Ukraine. Hall can feel his father is there with him as well. It’s as if his father’s life has joined with his own now that his spirit has moved on to the next world, into heaven. His father gives him strength. His daughter is there with him, and so is his father.

Fox News loves Ben Hall, and his courage and strength inspire all of us.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DR. MARC SIEGEL

Marc Siegel, M.D. is a professor of medicine and medical director of Doctor Radio at NYU Langone Medical Center. He is Fox News Channel's senior medical analyst. His forthcoming book is "The Angels Among Us: How God's Messengers Play a Role in Healing." (Fox Books, November 17, 2026). His previous book "The Miracles Among Us: How God's Grace Plays a Role in Healing" (Fox Books, November 18, 2025)  debuted at #1 on both the New York Times and Publisher’s Weekly bestseller lists. He is also the author of "COVID: The Politics of Fear and the Power of Science." Follow him on X @drmarcsiegel.

title: 'Lioness' star Zoe Saldaña says she can't imagine taking on another Taylor Sheridan role
excerpt:
Zoe Saldana admitted to Fox News Digital that she "wished" she knew how to balance raising her three sons while maintaining a career in Hollywood.

Zoe Saldaña has drawn the line when it comes to taki...
body_text:
Zoe Saldana admitted to Fox News Digital that she "wished" she knew how to balance raising her three sons while maintaining a career in Hollywood.

Zoe Saldaña has drawn the line when it comes to taking on more of Taylor Sheridan’s television empire.

The Oscar-winning actress, who leads Sheridan’s CIA drama "Lioness" as Joe McNamara, said the demanding role already pushes her to the limit – leaving little room to venture further into the prolific creator’s growing television universe.

"I think that Joe McNamara and 'Lioness' is all that I can handle at this time," she told People.

ZOE SALDAÑA SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES INSTAGRAM POSTS FROM BRUTAL 'LIONESS' TORTURE SCENE

Zoe Saldaña said starring as CIA operative Joe McNamara in Taylor Sheridan's "Lioness" has been so demanding that she has no interest in joining any of the prolific creator's other television series. (Ryan Green/Paramount+)

For Saldaña, carrying the series comes with a heavy workload long before cameras start rolling.

"I’m number one on the call sheet. I am first one in, last one out," she explained. "I am prepping months before anybody ever is able to prep. So it’s already a lot of work for me."

"I can’t imagine me taking on more of a Taylor Sheridan world," she said.

ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'REALLY SEES WOMEN' AS LIONESS SEASON THREE HITS PARAMOUNT+

Zoe Saldaña explained that leading the Paramount+ drama requires months of preparation and leaves her as the first person on set and the last to leave each day. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)

While Saldaña may not be looking for more work from Sheridan, she believes their three seasons together have earned his trust.

"The good takeaway that I’m grateful for is that he knows that I’m reliable, just like Joe is," she noted.

She claimed Sheridan knows she's "honest," "tough as nails" and "vocal and opinionated."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Zoe Saldaña also admitted she questioned whether she could handle the role before Season 3 premiered, calling it the most challenging performance of her career. (Ryan Green/Paramount+)

"I have my views, and I come with all heart, all brains, all muscle at all times," she explained. "So, no, I think I’m good here at 'Lioness.'"

Before Season three aired on Aug. 2, Saldaña admitted she had doubts about whether she could handle everything the role required.

"It was very demanding, I’m not gonna lie," she told Entertainment Weekly at the time. "I didn’t even know if I was gonna be able to pull it off."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Zoe Saldaña praised Taylor Sheridan for writing Joe as a character defined by her abilities rather than her gender, saying she was honored to portray one of his female leads. (Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic via Getty Images)

Season three ended Sept. 20, but Paramount+ has not yet greenlit the series for a Season four.

In Season three, Joe’s dangerous CIA career became intensely personal in the last episodes. The season put her family and marriage under mounting pressure while Joe herself became a target. Saldaña has described portraying Joe as the most challenging role of her career.

Part of what makes Joe stand out for Saldaña is that Sheridan didn't define the character by her gender.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Zoe Saldaña's comments come after "Lioness" wrapped its third season on Sept. 20, while Paramount+ has yet to announce whether the series will return for a fourth season. (Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images)

"We’ve seen various stories of men like Joe," she told the outlet.

"When you write something so incredible that it kind of defies gender and race, and it’s just about the merit of that human being, I feel like you give yourself the opportunity of a wider range of actors that can come in and sort of vie for that part," Saldaña said.

"I have a great deal of respect for men that really know how to write women," she added. "I’m happy to say that, after playing one of his female characters for three seasons, I’m incredibly honored that he wrote Joe as a woman."

title: 'Nobody Wants This' star accuses Israel of 'genocide'
excerpt:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations against Israel at the UN General Assembly.

On Friday, Jewish actor Adam Brody joined the growing list of progressive celebrities...
body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations against Israel at the UN General Assembly.

On Friday, Jewish actor Adam Brody joined the growing list of progressive celebrities accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza while suggesting that Hollywood has grown more "conservative" under President Donald Trump.

Brody, who plays a rabbi in Netflix’s romantic comedy series "Nobody Wants This," addressed the topic when speaking to GQ Magazine about his political activism and volunteer work for the progressive organization Swing Left. Although he has not publicly addressed the Middle East conflict previously, Brody told the magazine that he has discussed it privately.

"Put me down as thinking it's a genocide," Brody said. "Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It's awful that it's taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it's reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I'm hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is."

FORMULA ONE DRIVER LEWIS HAMILTON TELLS MACKLEMORE HE IS ‘STANDING’ IN SOLIDARITY WITH HIM ON PALESTINE

U.S. actor Adam Brody spoke to GQ Magazine about his political activism. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images)

"The O.C." actor's comments resembled ones made by other progressive celebrities such as actor Mark Ruffalo and rapper Macklemore, who have referred to the Israel-Hamas conflict as a "genocide."

Though several celebrities have spoken out against Israel's actions, Brody suggested that political activism in Hollywood has decreased, noting that he doesn't speak about political issues in many interviews.

"I think it's the cycle. The first time Trump was elected, it was inconceivable. It woke everyone," he said. "There was so much activism. People were running for office that had never ran before. It was so awful to watch him defile our government, our country, our reputation, and really pit people against each other. I felt like most of the country right away was really against it."

"It felt very safe to step out against him in the first presidency," Brody continued. "The second time, the presidency was more powerful. Corporations were lining up behind him like they hadn't before. People had to risk more to get in front of it. It just felt like the mood wasn't there. The country decided this is the way it wants to go. As we start to pick up steam for this election, it's getting exciting again. We're starting to feel powerful again."

'SHE-HULK' STAR SLAMS TOM SELLECK, MICHAEL JORDAN AS 'COWARDLY' FOR AVOIDING POLITICAL TALK

Several progressive celebrities have called for a "free Palestine" and accused Israel of committing "genocide. (Attila Husejnow/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Brody even claimed that Hollywood has gotten more "outspokenly" conservative during Trump's second term.

"Again, as one side has more power, it makes sense that it draws people to it for all the human reasons that would be attractive: groupthink, your own well-being, your own money and success," Brody said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Brody's representatives for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

In response to the interview, "Hollywood in Toto" founder Christian Toto told Fox News Digital that while it has gotten "microscopically better" to be a conservative in Hollywood, groupthink and bullying behind the scenes "remain powerful" as activism starts to see a resurgence.

MICHAEL RAPAPORT TELLS CRAIG CARTON THAT HIS SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL HAS COST HIM WORK IN HOLLYWOOD

Christian Toto disagreed with Adam Brody's suggestion that Hollywood is more conservative under President Donald Trump. (iStock; Getty Images)

"Hollywood activism was a bit muted following the 2024 election, but now it's back to its usual volume and cadence. And if Brody truly felt afraid to say what he's saying ... he would keep it all to himself. Sharing his doctrinaire, hard-Left views is the most pro-career move an actor can make in 2026, particularly in how he's viewed by fellow actors," Toto said.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

title: Olise scores late to grab France 1-0 Nations League win at Belgium
excerpt:
Michael Olise’s magnificent late strike gave France a 1-0 victory in Belgium in the UEFA Nations League as Zinedine Zidane made it two wins out of two since being named coach.

Bayern Munich star Olis...
body_text:
Michael Olise’s magnificent late strike gave France a 1-0 victory in Belgium in the UEFA Nations League as Zinedine Zidane made it two wins out of two since being named coach.

Bayern Munich star Olise, who was one of the outstanding players at the World Cup where France reached the semifinals, came off the bench late on with the game in Brussels on Monday goalless, and set off from inside his own half to score the winner in the 88th minute.

The win follows a 1-0 success away to Turkiye last Friday in Zidane’s first game at the helm after succeeding Didier Deschamps as France coach following the World Cup.

France are therefore top of Nations League Group A1 with six points, three points ahead of Belgium and Italy, with the latter winning 4-1 in Turkiye on Monday.

Les Bleus play host to Italy next at the Stade de France on Friday in what will be Zidane’s homecoming. France will then entertain Belgium on October 5.

Zidane was without captain Kylian Mbappe, with the Real Madrid striker having returned to his club for treatment after injuring his left knee while scoring the winner against Turkiye.

The French lineup at the King Baudouin Stadium showed nine changes, with goalkeeper Mike Maignan and Chelsea defender Maxence Lacroix the only players to keep their places.

There was notably a debut in midfield for Lucas Da Cunha of Como in Italy, as well as in attack for Esteban Lepaul of Rennes, the top scorer in France’s Ligue 1 last season.

Belgium, in contrast, made only two changes to the team that started during Friday’s 2-0 win in Italy for what was new coach Mark van Bommel’s home bow.

France had the better of the chances with Paris Saint-Germain’s Desire Doue cracking a shot off the bar in the first half and Da Cunha striking the post early in the second half.

But the contest was heading to an unremarkable goalless conclusion until Olise intervened, having been sent on in the 77th minute in place of Liverpool winger Bradley Barcola.

The London-born player collected possession inside his own half and advanced all the way to the edge of the Belgian box before curling a shot beyond the reach of Senne Lammens into the bottom-left corner of the net.

title: El-Sayed questions ethics of football in resurfaced audio
excerpt: Abdul El-Sayed faces intense criticism as Sean Hannity exposes the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee's controversial past comments. In unearthed videos from 2024, El-Sayed claims fireworks are harmfu...
body_text:
Abdul El-Sayed faces intense criticism as Sean Hannity exposes the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee's controversial past comments. In unearthed videos from 2024, El-Sayed claims fireworks are harmful and labels football as a sport defined by toxic masculinity.

Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed took aim at football culture, questioning whether America's most popular sport is "ethical," according to a resurfaced audio clip posted online Monday by the Republican Party.

In a 2023 podcast episode, the Michigan Democrat questioned whether American football could be considered "ethical" or "safe" due to the risk of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) for players and perceived ties to toxic masculinity and violence.

"What is it about this brutal sport that keeps us coming back?" El-Sayed is heard saying. "Is there a version of football that's actually ethical and safe? What would need to change?"

El-Sayed has questioned the sport in the past, most recently earlier this month when he released a video voicing concerns about the cost to attend NFL games.

ABDUL EL-SAYED DODGES 'RACIST NFL' CLAIM, CONTINUES DEFENDING COLIN KAEPERNICK

Abdul El-Sayed has questioned football's safety and ethics despite playing the sport growing up. (Abdul El-Sayed)

The video shows El-Sayed throwing and catching a football while questioning the high prices of tickets, in addition to money spent on concessions.

NEW RESEARCH FINDS 1 IN 4 NFL PLAYERS COULD DEVELOP CTE IN THEIR LIFETIME: 'SHOULD BE A CALL TO ACTION'

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks to reporters on the campaign trail in Lansing, Michigan. (Fox News Digital/Paul Steinhauser)

"It's gotten way too expensive," he said. "That means that something that's supposed to bring us all together, like football, separates those who have and those who have not."

He also noted that many football stadiums are subsidized by taxpayer funds, and yet, ticket prices continue to climb.

In October 2021, El-Sayed wrote that "the toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport — and men’s sports culture more generally — is way deeper than a few emails or a Jay-Z turnaround."

The Democratic Senate hopeful played football growing up and was the captain of his high school team. He called sports his "lifeline."

Despite his criticism of what he described as the toxic elements of male sports culture, El-Sayed has also defended masculinity and chided Democrats for talking down to men, often posting fitness-related content as part of his strategy to appeal to male voters.

Fox News Digital has reached out to El-Sayed for comment.

Woman waves knife after stabbing 2, killing a Bank of America vice president. (NYPD)

Newly released NYPD body camera footage shows officers pleading with the woman they say fatally stabbed a New Jersey mother in Times Square to drop two knives and "just breathe" moments before police opened fire.

Police released the video Friday, showing officers spending about four minutes trying to calm 49-year-old Pamela Cisneros outside One Times Square after she allegedly stabbed two people minutes earlier.

During the standoff, Cisneros repeatedly refused commands to surrender, told officers she was "tired of this world" and said they would have to kill her.

NYPD IDENTIFIES WOMAN KILLED IN TIMES SQUARE STABBING SPREE

"There's a lot to live for," one officer told Cisneros.

An NYPD officer speaks with Pamela Cisneros as she stands holding two knives outside One Times Square in Manhattan on Aug. 31, 2026. (NYPD)

"The world is hard. Especially New York City," the officer continued. "Trust me, we all suffer. But this is not the way."

As officers continued working to build rapport, one asked whether she believed in God.

VIOLENT TRANSIT ATTACKS IN ATLANTA, NEW YORK AND CHARLOTTE FUEL CALLS FOR TOUGHER TRACKING OF REPEAT OFFENDERS

NYPD body camera footage shows officers confronting Pamela Cisneros outside One Times Square in Manhattan on Aug. 31, 2026, moments after authorities say she fatally stabbed a woman and injured another victim. (NYPD)

Officers repeatedly assured Cisneros they wanted to help.

"We're trying to help you," one officer said.

NYPD OFFICERS FATALLY SHOOT MAN ARMED WITH BUTCHER KNIFE AFTER HE ADVANCED TOWARD COPS: POLICE

The encounter grew more tense when Cisneros told officers they would have to kill her.

"You're going to have to kill me," she said.

KNIFE-WIELDING MAN RACES AT OFFICER IN PACKED SEASIDE PARK BEFORE ONE DEADLY SHOT RINGS OUT: VIDEO

Moments later, she added, "Either that or I'm going to kill all of you."

Multiple NYPD officers surround Pamela Cisneros outside One Times Square during a standoff before police fatally shot her on Aug. 31, 2026. (NYPD)

Police continued ordering Cisneros to "drop the knife" and "just breathe" as she refused to surrender.

NYPD OFFICER SHOT, GUNMAN KILLED AFTER ARMED BARRICADED STANDOFF IN BROOKLYN: POLICE

Around 4:29 p.m., officers deployed Tasers after Cisneros began waving both knives. When the devices failed to stop her and she advanced toward officers with the blades pointed at them, police opened fire, striking her. She was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

NYPD body camera footage shows officers confronting Pamela Cisneros outside One Times Square moments before police opened fire on Aug. 31, 2026. (NYPD)

Police recovered both knives at the scene.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Authorities said the confrontation began minutes after Cisneros stabbed a 68-year-old man near West 41st Street and Seventh Avenue, seriously injuring him.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

She then walked north while carrying a knife in each hand before fatally stabbing 32-year-old Erin Piacenti, of Chester, New Jersey, near West 42nd Street about 20 seconds later.

Erin Piacenti, the Bank of America Vice President who was killed in a stabbing attack in New York City's Times Square on Monday Aug. 31, 2026. (Facebook/Erin Piacenti)

MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY

Transit officers encountered Cisneros outside One Times Square about a minute later and repeatedly ordered her to drop the knives while attempting to engage her in conversation. Additional officers soon arrived and joined the effort to de-escalate the confrontation.

Piacenti, a Bank of America executive and Fordham Law graduate, had returned to work just days earlier after spending five months on maternity leave caring for her newborn daughter. She died from her injuries. The 68-year-old man survived after suffering a stab wound to the abdomen.

A photo showing two knives recovered at the scene is displayed during a press conference following a fatal stabbing incident in Times Square near West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue in Manhattan, New York, United States, on August 31, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Police have described the attacks as random and unprovoked.

The NYPD said Cisneros had documented mental health-related encounters with the department in 2018 and 2019 but no prior arrest record. There was no indication the attack was related to terrorism.

The NYPD's Force Investigation Division continues to investigate the shooting before the case is presented to the department's Use of Force Review Board.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

title: French far-right leader Bardella refutes anti-Semitism allegations
excerpt:
The president of France’s far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN), Jordan Bardella, has denied allegations of anti-Semitism.

Bardella’s refutation on Monday followed the publication o...
body_text:
The president of France’s far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN), Jordan Bardella, has denied allegations of anti-Semitism.

Bardella’s refutation on Monday followed the publication of a report by the Mediapart outlet alleging that the politician sent anti-Semitic private messages a decade ago. The report emerged shortly after RN secured a record 14 seats in the Senate, confirming its strong prospects ahead of presidential elections early next year.

“I formally dispute the accusations against me by Mediapart, which attributes to me deranged and anti-Semitic remarks that I supposedly made when I was a minor. These are obviously blatant forgeries,” Bardella wrote on social media.

The 31-year-old politician, a close ally of presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, claimed that the “activist press” is orchestrating “smear operations” to “destabilise” RN’s presidential campaign, just as “the victory of our ideas has never been so close”.

Bardella, tipped to become prime minister should Le Pen win the presidency, said he had instructed his lawyer ⁠to pursue “all necessary proceedings”.

Mediapart said it has reviewed dozens of private messages from 2013-2015 that depict a pattern of anti-Semitic rhetoric. The report cites one message in which Bardella allegedly claimed “all the banks are owned by Jews”.

“Since I began engaging in politics, I have never had any ambiguity about the fight against anti-Semitism and was received by the Israeli government in 2025,” Bardella told the right-wing French media outlet CNews.

Mediapart wrote that in a chat, Bardella had said: “The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so.”

The left-leaning outlet said it had independently authenticated the private messages and had also drawn on testimony from former party colleagues.

The youthful Bardella has led the RN party’s rebrand as it seeks to break from racist and anti-Semitic history it developed when it was named the National Front. The party, founded by Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie, and led by Marine from 2011 to 2021, changed its name in 2018.

A slew of anti-Semitic, Islamophobic and racist comments by candidates impacted the party’s ⁠chances of winning a parliamentary majority in France’s legislative vote in 2024.

Bardella at the time pledged to avoid what he called “casting errors” by systematically kicking out candidates with a history of toxic statements.

He was the party’s de facto presidential candidate until July, when an appeals court cleared Marine Le Pen to run for the presidency.

On Monday, she said the report could “only be a fake, a manipulation, a dirty trick”, adding that she expects Bardella to file an imminent defamation lawsuit.

Le Pen has also sought to clear the party’s racist image and emphasised building closer ties with Israel.

title: Cam Ward's sister says her family has been target of 'threats, harassment' by fans angry about brother's play
excerpt:
NFL Hall of Famer and former Chicago Bears linebacker defends Caleb Williams from backlash over his reaction to a hamstring injury, but says the incident "could have been handled different."

The pric...
body_text:
NFL Hall of Famer and former Chicago Bears linebacker defends Caleb Williams from backlash over his reaction to a hamstring injury, but says the incident "could have been handled different."

The price of celebrity and a big-dollar NFL contract for Tennessee Titans starting quarterback Cam Ward is apparently being paid, in part, by his family. They have been the target of "threats, harassment, and bullying," according to his sister.

Chantel Ward says she is one of the targets because her brother is obviously not playing up to the expectations of being the team's 2025 first-round Draft pick.

She laid bare her feelings on the issue on Monday — not coincidentally after Ward struggled in the winless Titans' 12-7 loss at home to the New York Giants.

"The fact I even have to post this is diabolical," Ward, the player's 27-year-old older sister, posted on her Instagram account.

IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?

Apr 24, 2025; Green Bay, WI, USA; Miami Hurricanes quarterback Cameron Ward holds the jersey on stage after he is selected by the Tennessee Titans as the number one pick in the first round of the 2025 NFL Draft at Lambeau Field. (Kirby Lee-Imagn Images)

"People see the football games. They see the wins, the losses, the interceptions, the touchdowns, the press conferences and everything that happens on the field. What they don't see is what comes with it for the people who love these players when the game is over."

What typically happens is the families of well-paid players who were drafted first overall, as Ward was, live a privileged life.

But there's more, according to Chantel Ward. Because that life has its obstacles and major concerns.

And getting online threats has apparently become one of those for the Wards.

WILL LEVIS SUPREMELY CONFIDENT HE IS CAPABLE OF BEING NFL STARTER WHILE BATTLING FOR TITANS' BACKUP ROLE

Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) loses the ball after being pressured by Houston Texans defensive end Danielle Hunter, left, during the first half of an NFL football game Sunday, Sept. 28, 2025, in Houston. (AP Photo/David J. Phillip)

"After games, people come directly to my DMs on Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram with threats, hate, bullying, personal attacks, and disrespect toward me and my family – all over football," she wrote.

Ward made the point that it is fair to be critical of players because that's part of the sport. Play good, all good.

"Criticize the game," Ward wrote. "Criticize a play. Be frustrated with your team. That's sports, and I completely understand that. But seeking out a player's sister, parents, or other family members to personally attack them because you're upset about what happened on a football field is something completely different.

"Cam is a quarterback to y'all. He's entertainment on Sundays. To me, that's my little brother. Somebody I've loved, protected, supported, and watched work for his entire life.

Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) runs the ball during the second quarter of an NFL pre-season game against the Minnesota Vikings at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tenn., Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. (IMAGN)

SOME TITANS PLAYERS ARRIVE AT THEIR GAME SUNDAY AGAINST THE EAGLES LOOKING RIDICULOUS

"So when people come to my page or into my messages is disrespecting him, me or my family, and then tell me, 'Don't take it personal' – how exactly am I supposed to take it?

"And trust me, the screenshots I share are only a fraction of what comes through. There's so much that happens outside of those football games that people will never see."

Ward shared a screenshot on her story of someone who answered and said her brother "shouldn't play like a f——-g r — —d and people would come in here and congratulate you."

Ward did not share a post proving the family has received threats, but she made the allegation that she's flooded by them.

Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) walks off the field after the team's loss in an NFL football game against the Houston Texans, Sunday, Sept. 28, 2025, in Houston. (AP Photo/David J. Phillip)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"Criticize football all you want," she wrote. "Criticize performance. Criticize the decisions. That comes with the territory.

"But threats, harassment, bullying, and attacking someone's family will never be just part of the game."

One more thing: If the Wards are indeed enduring threats online and are afraid those might manifest where they live, they should contact authorities.

At minimum, the quarterback should alert the Titans.

It's unclear if that has happened. The Titans did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.
