excerpt:
Buses for London aims for ‘greener, safer and better-value’ service but private operators say move will not fix problems

London buses in decline? Why public transport is slowing to a crawl – visualis...
body_text:
Buses for London aims for ‘greener, safer and better-value’ service but private operators say move will not fix problems

London buses in decline? Why public transport is slowing to a crawl – visualised

A publicly owned company, Buses for London, will start running services in the capital next year, Transport for London has announced.

TfL said the launch was a “major milestone” in its plans to improve buses for drivers and passengers.

The new public company will take over a handful of London’s bus routes, which number nearly 700 in total, from late 2027, starting with route 6, which runs between Willesden and Victoria station.

A further four routes to be run by the public company from 2028 are to be announced.

TfL said the creation of a publicly owned bus company would give it greater control over how services were run, allowing it to make buses more reliable and safe, and to reinvest profits into improving the transport network.

At present, TfL contracts bus services to eight privately owned operators.

The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “This is an opportunity to reimagine our bus network so that it provides better value for money, supports our climate goals, makes our roads safer, and overall just works better for passengers and drivers alike.”

London’s buses have been getting gradually slower and passenger numbers have fallen over the past decade, as they battle with congestion and demands on road space in the capital.

Lorna Murphy, TfL’s director of buses, said the public company marked “an exciting new chapter”, with a depot in the Old Oak regeneration area that would be “the first home of a new generation of zero-emission buses … helping us to build on the progress we’ve already made towards a more sustainable transport system”.

Unions welcomed the move but private operators said the taxpayer would foot the bill for investment and take on more risk.

The Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “Unite has long been calling for London’s bus services to be returned to public ownership. Outsourcing to private companies hasn’t worked well for workers or passengers.

“For too long, bus workers have been subjected to intolerable working conditions and passengers have experienced worsening services, while bus firms and their shareholders rake in huge profits.”

The union’s national officer for passenger transport, Wayne King, said it was “only the beginning”. He said Unite expected Buses for London to “lead the way in workers’ pay, terms and conditions and treatment and will hold TfL and the mayor to account on this”.

The Confederation of Passenger Transport, representing bus firms, said it would not fix London’s buses. Graham Vidler, the chief executive of CPT, said: “Passengers don’t need a new public bus operator. They need faster, more reliable journeys and investment should be made where passengers will actually feel the difference: tackling congestion, giving buses priority and getting London moving.

“Regardless of who operates the service, buses typically travel at just 9 mph in London – slower than the average cyclist.”

He said private operators had made significant investment in London’s bus network, including new vehicles and technology, adding: “The uncertainty created by a new publicly owned operator risks making it harder for private operators to make the case for continued investment in London in the future.”

Labour’s bus overhauls since 2025, which push wider franchising and public control of services, have also made it possible for local authorities nationwide to establish new publicly owned companies. A few municipal companies, such as Reading, Blackpool and Nottingham, survived deregulation and privatisation in the 1980s.

title: Fighter jet pilots eject moments before fiery crash in Wales
excerpt:
Video captures moment two Royal Air Force pilots ejected from a training aircraft before a fiery crash in Wales. (Credit: Danni Jones via Storyful)

A video captured the moment two Royal Air Force pil...
body_text:
Video captures moment two Royal Air Force pilots ejected from a training aircraft before a fiery crash in Wales. (Credit: Danni Jones via Storyful)

A video captured the moment two Royal Air Force pilots ejected from a training aircraft before a fiery crash in Wales.

The Royal Air Force (RAF) said the incident involving a Hawk T2 aircraft happened near Anglesey on Wednesday after the pilots departed the RAF Valley base in the northwestern part of the country.

"Both pilots are doing well, they are in extremely good spirits and expected to make a full recovery," the RAF said in a statement. "A formal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident is now underway and as a precautionary measure, the RAF has temporarily paused Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 flying operations."

BLOODIED, EJECTED MARINE CORPS PILOT SEEN CALM AND COLLECTED AFTER WASHINGTON CRASH DESTROYS AIRCRAFT

A Royal Air Force Hawk T2 training aircraft crashed in Wales on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Danni Jones via Storyful)

Footage taken by local resident Danni Jones and obtained by Storyful shows the pilots parachuting through the air after a fireball erupted in the Welsh countryside.

The RAF said on its website that the Hawk T2 "is a high-performance, 2-seat training jet equipped with advanced avionics and synthetic radar to simulate front-line combat aircraft like the Typhoon."

PILOT EJECTS AS F-35 CRASHES AT MCAS MIRAMAR, SPARKING FIRE

The Royal Air Force BAE Systems Hawk T2 participates is seen at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, on July 20, 2024. (NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"Used primarily by the RAF for advanced jet training, it prepares pilots for complex tactical environments," it added.

The cause of Wednesday's crash was not immediately clear.

A Royal Air Force British Aerospace Hawk T2 flies along the Machynlleth Loop, a set of valleys in north Wales where pilots train in low-level flying, on March 27, 2023. (AFP via Getty Images)

"RAF Valley on Anglesey is home to No 4 Flying Training School, responsible for training the UK's next generation of world-class fighter pilots," according to the RAF. "Aircrew are also trained at RAF Valley for mountain and maritime operations throughout the world."

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: '80s star Tiffany steps into dream role after leaving Hollywood behind
excerpt:
Tiffany Darwish told Fox News Digital that by 6 PM everyday, she is in the kitchen cooking before a peaceful night.

'80s pop icon Tiffany is stepping back into the spotlight as she fulfills a dream s...
body_text:
Tiffany Darwish told Fox News Digital that by 6 PM everyday, she is in the kitchen cooking before a peaceful night.

'80s pop icon Tiffany is stepping back into the spotlight as she fulfills a dream she had prior to becoming a teen idol.

The 54-year-old singer, who rose to fame in 1987 after her song "I Think We're Alone Now" became a massive hit, made her Off-Broadway debut in "Spandex the Musical" last week.

During a July interview with People magazine, Tiffany reflected on why taking the stage felt like a "true full-circle moment for me."

'80S POP STAR TIFFANY EMBRACES QUIET NASHVILLE ROUTINE AFTER LEAVING CALIFORNIA BEHIND FOR GOOD

"Before music came into my life, I was a dancer and an actor, and those dreams were put on hold when ‘I Think We’re Alone Now’ took off and my recording career began," she said.

'80s icon Tiffany is stepping back into the spotlight to fulfill her lifelong dream after leaving Hollywood. (Bruce Glikas/Getty Images; Frank Hempel/United Archives via Getty Images)

Tiffany, whose full name is Tiffany Darwish, launched her career with the now-legendary Shopping Mall Tour '87, performing free concerts at malls across the country beginning in June 1987. The grassroots campaign helped turn the then-15-year-old into a teen sensation before she became a chart-topping artist.

In September 1987, Tiffany's cover of Tommy James and the Shondells' 1967 hit "I Think We're Alone Now" climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 less than two months after its release and made her a household name.

"I Think We're Alone Now" was the second single released from her self-titled debut album. She followed up with "Could've Been," the third single released from "Tiffany," which also topped the Billboard Hot 100. In addition, the album produced her Beatles cover "I Saw Him Standing There," which peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100, and "Feelings of Forever," which reached the No. 50 spot.

Tiffany rose to fame at 15 with her hit song "I Think We're Alone Now." (Ron Eisenberg/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

At 16, Tiffany became the youngest female artist to top the Billboard 200 with a debut album. She went on to headline her first major tour in 1988, with New Kids on the Block opening for her before the boy band's own meteoric rise.

However, Tiffany's chart dominance proved difficult to sustain. While her 1988 sophomore album, "Hold an Old Friend's Hand," was certified platinum by the RIAA and produced the Top 10 hit "All This Time," it fell short of matching the success of her debut. As the teen-pop landscape shifted in the early 1990s, her third album, "New Inside," failed to gain commercial traction.

RICK MORANIS, CAMERON DIAZ AND LINDSAY LOHAN AMONG STARS WHO LEFT FAME BEHIND BEFORE RETURNING TO HOLLYWOOD

In 1993, Tiffany released her fourth album, "Dreams Never Die," which was issued only in Asian markets. Afterward, Tiffany largely stepped back from the mainstream music scene to focus on raising her son Elijah, whom she shares with her ex-husband, makeup artist Bulmaro Garcia. The two were married from 1992 to 2003.

In the early 2000s, Tiffany left Hollywood behind and moved to Nashville. During a 2023 interview with Fox News Digital, she explained why she decided to embrace a simpler life in Tennessee.

She became the youngest female artist to have an album top the Billboard 200. (Paul Massey/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)

DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME

"I came to Nashville for the first time when I was 10," the California native recalled. "I’ve been coming back ever since. I love being out in the country – I’m a country girl at heart. I’ve toured all over the world and this place has always been home for me. There’s just something about coming home to my little ranch… I’ve never looked back."

Since the days of her teenage stardom, Tiffany has continued to tour and release music as an independent artist. She has also made appearances in movies and television shows and starred in several reality TV series.

During a June interview with Fox News Digital, Tiffany detailed how she spent the past several years building a culinary brand that combines her love of cooking, entertaining and connecting with fans. Through her platform, "Let's Food With Tiffany," she offers recipes, virtual cooking experiences and food-focused events that showcase the same energy and creativity that made her a pop sensation.

Earlier this year, Tiffany released her second cookbook, "POP LIFE: The Ultimate ‘80s Kitchen Encore," which she created with Las Vegas celebrity chef Alicia Shevetone. "POP LIFE: The Ultimate ’80s Kitchen Encore" followed her first cookbook, "Breakfast with Tiffany," which she released independently.

Tiffany left Hollywood for Nashville in the early 2000s. (Lorne Thomson /Darlene Hammond)

In July, Tiffany announced that she would make her New York theatrical debut in "Spandex the Musical," in which she plays Linda Gustafson, a housewife who competes in the fictional 1988 Crystal Light National Aerobics Championship.

"I’ve always believed the right role would find me, and the moment I read the script, I knew Linda was that character," she told People magazine at the time.

"Just as Linda discovers a new passion through aerobics that changes her life, I’ve found exciting new passions beyond music through my ‘Pop Life’ cookbook, ‘Let’s Food With Tiffany’ events, and now returning to acting on stage," she continued. "It’s a reminder that it’s never too late to reinvent yourself."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Spandex: The Musical" is a 10-day limited Off-Broadway engagement which runs through Sept. 27. After each performance, Tiffany performs "I Think We're Alone Now" during the curtain call.

She is currently starring in Off-Broadway's "Spandex: The Musical." (Bruce Glikas/Getty Images)

"There are so many wonderful parallels between Linda’s journey and my own, and I’m thrilled the producers have even woven in some fun Tiffany Easter eggs that I know longtime fans are going to love," she told People.

Tiffany said the project is especially meaningful because a portion of the show's proceeds will benefit Children's Miracle Network, a nonprofit organization that raises money for 170 children's hospitals across the United States and Canada.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Tiffany said that the role is a "dream come true." (Bruce Glikas/Getty Images)

"Making my Off-Broadway debut with such a funny, heartfelt and uplifting show is truly a dream come true," Tiffany said. "I’m also incredibly proud that ‘Spandex The Musical’ is partnering with Children’s Miracle Network, with a portion of the proceeds helping children and families in need."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Giving back has always been close to my heart, so being able to combine my love of performing with a cause that means so much to me makes this experience even more special," she added.

"I can’t wait for audiences to experience the laughs, the music, the ‘80s nostalgia and, of course, plenty of spandex!"

Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: ‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate science
excerpt:
Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions

A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarc...
body_text:
Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions

A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months.

The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth.

Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross.

The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks.

Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.”

She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months.

The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction.

“It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.”

Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play in global heating.

“The ocean is doing all of us a great service by absorbing about a third of anthropogenic or human emissions every year,” Shadwick said, and the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, played a significant role. “If we want to continue to rely on this ocean service of absorbing our human emissions, we need to understand how it might change in the future.”

Crewed research vessels that travelled between Hobart and Antarctica traversed only a limited patch of the ocean, she said. The autonomous craft would gather data over a greater distance and time, including crucial measurements during the polar winter.

The vessel is the first in a fleet of four. Others are planned to be launched at three-monthly intervals. They will be spread across the Southern, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, particularly during winter.

The scientists will be able to access information in near real time via a mission portal, and once the vessels return to home base, all data and observations will undergo quality checks before they are made available for further research.

Dr Pep Canadell, a chief research scientist at the CSIRO, said for every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, about 500kg were removed by ocean and forest sinks. “This is like a 50% discount on climate change,” he said.

But the amount absorbed by the oceans could change due to multiple drivers: warming waters, westerly winds, melting ice, ocean acidification and the hole in the ozone layer. Observations would enable scientists to more accurately model these processes and understand how they could change in the future, he said.

The University of New South Wales professor Matthew England, who studies the role of ocean circulation in global climate but was not involved in the research project, said measuring how much the oceans absorbed and how that was changing was critical.

“We’ve obviously got a surge of emissions going into our atmosphere. Both the terrestrial vegetation on land and the oceans absorb a big chunk of that,” he said. “We need to track that carbon uptake and understand exactly how big the absorption is. If it starts to decline in a significant way, then it tells us that we have an even bigger problem of carbon emission reductions.”

The Southern Ocean was “inhospitable” with huge swells, gale force winds, sea ice and storms. “These are very tough measuring conditions for a research vessel.” So gathering data using an autonomous vehicle, without burning fuel, was “an incredible deployment of technology”, he said.

title: NSW crackdown on ‘AI-doctored’ real estate listings hits mural-covered wall
excerpt:
Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fake

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The New ...
body_text:
Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fake

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales government’s crackdown on “AI-doctored” rental listings has hit a wall, after it made an example of a supposedly manipulated ad that turned out to be a genuine photograph of a $5,000 courtyard mural of Bondi beach.

In a media release on Friday announcing protections against misleading rental ads, the state government provided a link to a property in Leichhardt, claiming it was an “AI-doctored rental listing in Sydney’s Inner West”.

But the listing agency IB Property denied the images were altered.

A spokesperson confirmed the photograph shows a mural of Bondi beach on an internal courtyard wall visible through the unit’s windows, rather than a false digital depiction of coastal views.

“We can confirm that the image has not been altered or digitally generated using AI, Photoshop or any other image-editing software,” the spokesperson said.

Leichhardt is about 12km away from Bondi beach.

When Guardian Australia visited 2/14 Norton Street, the artwork was not visible from the street. IB Property explained the mural sits within an internal courtyard and provided photos taken inside the unit confirming it remains in place.

“The mural was commissioned and paid for by the landlord at a cost of approximately $5,000, and we can also confirm that there are no plans for it to be removed,” the spokesperson said, adding that the property was leased in February 2026 and has not been advertised since.

The better regulation and fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose office issued the media release, didn’t respond directly to questions from Guardian Australia, but did issue the following statement:

“Every renter knows the frustration of seeing a property online, only to turn up and find it looks nothing like the listing.

“These laws are about putting an end to misleading practices and making sure renters get a fair go. We will always stand on the side of renters.”

Despite the mix-up, the new laws target an increasing market issue.

Under the legislation, real estate businesses in NSW will face fines of up to $22,000 for failing to disclose digitally altered or AI-generated property images.

The bill targets the rapid rise of “housefishing” – where digital alterations distort the true size and condition of a home.

Chanthivong said the new laws would establish strong protections against misleading property marketing and support ethical AI use. The regulations take effect in early 2027.

The legislation arrives as generative AI embeds itself in property marketing nationwide.

Tim McKibbin, the chief executive of the Real Estate Institute of NSW, said generative AI complicates pre-existing digital enhancement in the industry.

“This technology has been available for some years now … people have used Photoshop,” he said. “People were removing trees and removing telegraph poles … clearly that is false and misleading.”

McKibbin draws a line between virtual staging and false advertising. “I’ve seen instances where agents have put furniture into the photographs … Now, that is merely giving you an indication of what you could do,” he said.

Stewart Bunn, of First National Real Estate, said consumer trust is being tested by poor industry examples, referencing a 2024 instance where an LJ Hooker branch used AI to generate a listing with nonexistent schools.

“We have seen examples across the industry where AI-generated images have depicted renovations that have not occurred, furnishings that create an unrealistic impression of scale, landscaping that does not exist or finishes that materially differ from the actual property,” Bunn said.

“The best practice is simple: if a buyer would be surprised by what they see when they arrive at the property, the advertising has gone too far.”

An RMIT University report led by Dr Leah Li, funded by the Australian Property Institute, found a “significant lack of sector-specific AI frameworks to guide responsible AI practice within the property profession”.

Public confidence remains fragile: a 2026 Cotality study showed only 40% of Australians trust AI-generated outputs, compared with 62% in Canada, 52% in the US, and 46% in the UK.

Dr Shuai Wang, a research fellow at the University of Queensland, said generative AI systems prioritise visual appeal over accuracy. In real estate, this can manifest as “hallucinations”.

“AI hallucinations can occur when AI-generated images introduce features that were never part of the property,” Li said, fundamentally changing a prospective tenant’s perception of “size, layout, condition, or amenity”.

Leo Patterson Ross, the chief executive of the Tenants’ Union of NSW, said deceptive imagery can artificially inflate rental markets by creating fake demand.

“By inflating the number of people who appear interested in a place and increasing pressure on someone to rush to put in an application or even offer above the advertised rent.”

Patterson Ross said stricter measures were necessary, rather than just disclosure. “The bill only requires disclosure of the use of digital alterations. We think any use of imagery that misrepresents the property should be disallowed.”

Li said long-term resolution will require national coordination combining “transparency requirements, professional accountability, industry standards, regulatory oversight, and consumer education”.

“Trust does not come from simply adopting AI; trust comes from transparency about how AI has been used and confidence that it is being used responsibly.”

For tenants navigating tight rental markets, AI distortion has added a frustrating layer of deception.

Roxanne Gardiner, 26, said AI-generated imagery was “rife” during her search for a rental in Brisbane’s eastern suburbs.

“I was constantly getting scammed by listing photos,” she said. “What’s so embarrassing is we didn’t even realise one of the first houses we saw was AI until we rocked up there.

“The AI furniture is not accurate to the rooms and would usually make them look bigger than they were.”

Beyond virtual staging, Gardiner observed artificial greenery and soft lighting that changed the true character of a home.

“It feels cheap … lazy and insulting,” she said. “We just stopped going to AI listings, period. We started asking: ‘What are they compensating for?’” Gardiner’s group eventually signed a lease on an unedited property within three days of manually filtering out AI-altered ads.

Matt Stitt, 25, faced similar issues searching in south Brisbane.

“Listings had completely replaced floorboards to look new, edited in area rugs that near-covered entire rooms,” he said. “It was such a waste of time seeing these haunted houses with a digital paint job.”

The NSW legislation also protects privacy for more than 2.3 million renters by curbing excessive data harvesting. Landlords and property managers must use standardised application forms, banning requests for personal photos, social media handles, tattoo details or children’s information.

Sensitive identity documents, such as driver’s licences and passports, will only be collected from the single preferred applicant prior to lease signing, eliminating roughly 187,000 document collections annually, according to the government.

Penalties for privacy breaches will reach up to $11,000 for individuals and $49,500 for corporations. The bill also mandates the disclosure of embedded utility networks upfront.

Chanthivong said privacy protections build on broader rental reforms, including fee-free payment options and ending no-grounds evictions.

“Whether you have a tattoo, or what school your kids go to, is not relevant to whether you’ll be a good tenant.”

title: US math and reading test scores are at a 25-year low. Trump cut the agency that can provide answers
excerpt:
National Center for Education Statistics, which collects critical data to guide policy on learning, was decimated after Doge canceled crucial contracts

As reading and math scores fall to their lowest...
body_text:
National Center for Education Statistics, which collects critical data to guide policy on learning, was decimated after Doge canceled crucial contracts

As reading and math scores fall to their lowest point in the past quarter-century, the US now has fewer tools to understand and develop interventions for this troubling trend.

When the Trump administration took a wrecking ball to the Department of Education last year, firing nearly half of its workers and allowing the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) to cancel nearly $900m in contracts, a little-known agency called the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) was among the hardest hit.

NCES, a federal statistical agency, has for decades collected critical data on the state of education in America, including The Nation’s Report Card, an assessment of what students know across math, reading, writing, science and history. NCES data also helps set US education policy and allocate funding for school districts.

But nearly all of the statistical agency’s work was abruptly terminated and its headcount dropped from about 100 to four. Some were rehired; NCES now has 12 staffers, according to the agency’s website.

The cuts, which are part of the administration’s broader attack on taxpayer-funded data and research that don’t align with the president’s priorities, have hamstrung the historically under-resourced agency’s ability to collect and report on a range of data on K-12 and college students. These include surveys on the prevalence of guns and violence at middle and high schools and studies on how students are paying for college, former NCES employees say.

Now, most of the agency’s ongoing data collections and reports appear to be inactive or reduced in scope, according to a tracker, based on publicly available information, published by the American Statistical Association. (The education department did not answer the Guardian’s questions about how many data collections have been terminated.)

Savannah Newhouse, an education department spokesperson, said in a statement to the Guardian that the Institute of Education Sciences (IES), the research and statistics arm of the education department that NCES is part of, is still collecting some data, including the National Assessment of Educational Progress , known as The Nation’s Report Card.

“The Trump administration is committed to ensuring that IES delivers usable, high-quality statistics, data and resources for educators, researchers and other stakeholders,” she wrote. “NCES and IES were in need of reform – and that work is well underway.”

But researchers and advocates say the cuts to NCES are coming at a time when it’s more critical than ever to have an objective measure of how American students are doing given the decline in math and literacy.

“Dismantling a statistical agency is just shooting the messenger,” said Carolyn Grim, who spent 15 years at NCES as an education statistician before retiring early in 2025. She’s now founder and executive director of the non-profit Agora Education Research. “It makes no more sense than saying: ‘I’m going to just fire my accountant because I can’t control my spending.’”

Much of the data terminated by Doge were longitudinal studies – studies that follow individual students for a period of time and allow researchers to see the effects of specific policies and understand the reasons behind trends such as declining reading scores.

For Peggy Carr, the former NCES commissioner, who was abruptly fired last spring after nearly four decades at the agency, “probably the most painful example” was the termination of the Early childhood longitudinal study (ECLS).

The ECLS followed thousands of students across the country from kindergarten through fifth grade, evaluated their academic achievement and surveyed their parents, teachers and school administrators.

Last winter, Doge canceled the $47m contract in the middle of the third iteration of the survey, which occurs roughly every decade. The study contractor, Westat, was preparing to follow up with a group of the 15,000 first graders it had surveyed in the fall of 2023, when the students were entering kindergarten, when the funding was suddenly cut.

This would have been the first survey of kids born after Covid, and included new questions tailored to understanding the effects of the pandemic, such as childcare arrangements and hybrid in-person and online instruction.

“We were going to study them into their first and third grade years to see how the pandemic influenced their development and their learning, but now we’ll never know because we’re not able to follow these children into the future,” Carr said.

Since it started in 1998, the ECLS has been cited in nearly 3,000 academic papers, including research on how early reading is a predictor of reading skill in later grades, the importance of developing executive function skills and the effects of full-day versus half-day kindergarten on reading and math learning.

“We as a country made huge investments in early childhood and we have all sorts of policies that get rolled out around introducing preschool, or Head Start, or different early interventions, and we basically don’t have a tool with which to say, OK, and to what extent did that work?” said Daphna Bassok, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies the outcomes of early childhood education policies.

In addition to the loss of data for research, advocates say the Trump administration’s cuts to education data let years of work and millions of government dollars go to waste.

Some longitudinal studies were canceled in the final years of data collection. That happened with the beginning postsecondary students (BPS) longitudinal study 20-25, which tracked more than 30,000 students who started college in the fall of 2019 through 2025, and the high school longitudinal study of 2009, which followed 23,000 ninth graders who started in 2009 all the way into their early 30s.

“These cuts were wasteful and didn’t really save taxpayer money because most of that work had already been done,” said Diane Cheng, vice-president for policy at the Institute for Higher Education Policy.

The education department also needed to pay several million-dollar termination fees to contractors. A large portion of funding was spent upfront even for studies that had just gotten off the ground, such as the ECLS.

“There’s a huge amount spent on development, like just setting up the sample, reaching out to the schools, reaching out to the families, the states, getting participation, setting up the questionnaires,” said one person familiar with the process. “All of that had to be done before any data was collected.”

Multiple groups, including Cheng’s, have since filed several lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s cuts to funding and staffing for education data and research, part of a wave of broader outcry from researchers, advocates, teachers and parents to the administration’s goal to completely eliminate the US Department of Education.

Since then, several NCES data collections have been reinstated, including the national postsecondary student aid survey, which is the primary way researchers know how students pay for college, and the baccalaureate and beyond longitudinal study, which measures outcomes of bachelor’s degree graduates for 10 years.

“We know that advocacy and litigation create important public pressure for the department to rethink its decisions and move forward with data collections that it canceled,” Cheng said.

The Guardian’s Deleted data series explores how critical US government information is being deleted and what the consequences will be, and will preserve or recreate lost datasets. If you know about any datasets, webpages or government materials that have been deleted or altered in the past year, or are willing to share how those changes affect you, we would love to hear from you. Please reach out at deleted-data@theguardian.com.

Chin...
body_text:
Towering teenager Zhang Zhanshuo became the first swimmer in history to win seven golds at a single Asian Games, while on the track, Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson powered to victory in the 100m.

China’s Zhang, 19, scorched to the men’s 400m freestyle title in the pool in Tokyo on Friday in a Games-record three minutes and 41.28 seconds.

He sat on the lane divider after the race and slowly counted off on his fingers all seven medals he had won.

Zhang also won individual golds in the 200m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, as well as three relays.

He said, after wrapping up a scintillating campaign, that it had been the “perfect week”.

“I think the most important thing is to stay grounded and focused, because the Asian Games are not my ultimate goal,” said Zhang, who stands 198cm (six feet, six inches).

With the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away, China won 30 of the 42 golds in the pool this week.

Their 13-year-old phenomenon Yu Zidi was the undoubted superstar, taking home three individual golds and all in Games-record times.

Not to be outdone, Japan’s 17-year-old Shin Ohashi shattered the men’s 200m breaststroke world record on Thursday.

Swimming, equestrian and diving are taking place in Tokyo, but the city of Nagoya and the wider Aichi prefecture are the main Games host.

The men’s and women’s 100m sprints, the blue riband events in track and field, took place in front of rows of empty seats in Nagoya.

China’s Chen Yujie streaked to a comfortable victory in the women’s final in a Games-record 11.06 seconds.

The men’s was won by 20-year-old Puripol, who burst out of the pack in the final quarter of the race to win in 9.90 seconds, breaking his Games record from earlier in the evening.

It was Thailand’s first men’s 100m gold medal since Suchart Jairsuraparp on home soil at the 1978 Bangkok Games.

On the last evening of gymnastics, Carlos Yulo won the men’s vault for his second gold of the Games.

The double Olympic champion won floor gold on Thursday to complete his collection of major titles.

“In this whole Asian Games, I felt really stressed, but at the same time, I enjoyed what I did today. I really did my part.

There’s little time to celebrate, however, with the world championships next month.

South Korea edged China 85-80 in the semifinals of the women’s basketball, and will face hosts Japan for gold.

China had their giant centre Zhang Ziyu, 19, but it was not enough.

Zhang Ziyu stands 223cm (seven feet, four inches) and scored 22 points.

“She was tough to guard,” said South Korea’s Kang Lee-seul.

“We couldn’t defend her, but we focused on fast breaks and shooting more three-pointers.”

North Korea’s women were again in record-setting form on the weightlifting dais.

Oh Kwang Ok set three world records on her way to women’s 57kg bodyweight class gold.

Oh lifted 104kg in the snatch and 134kg in the clean and jerk for a 238kg total – all world records to add to the two golds North Korea’s women won in the 49kg and 53kg classes this week.

North Korea has won four gold medals and two silvers in the six weightlifting events contested so far.

title: Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
excerpt:
The internet was cut in Tigray during the two-year civil war which ended in 2022 (file photo)

Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outb...
body_text:
The internet was cut in Tigray during the two-year civil war which ended in 2022 (file photo)

Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional forces and the national army.

Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray.

"Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.

The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.

Sources have told the Reuters news agency that the group which controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), ordered the communications blackout, with one suggesting it was to disrupt government drones.

The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.

Even before the current disruption, finding video and images to establish what is happening on the ground has been a challenge.

So far, other than footage from Mekelle, most of what has been shared online has been from outside the region.

The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one

Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody".

Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services.

On Thursday a Mekelle resident who we are only identifying as Fitsum made a similar point.

He told the BBC "there is almost no cash" in the city.

With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he said.

Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates

Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying.

A humanitarian source in the neighbouring region of Afar told the AFP news agency there was "heavy fighting overnight", including drone strikes, around the town of Abala in the mountains between Afar and Tigray, as "federal forces pushed the rebels from entering the town".

During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.

Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.

It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government.

On Wednesday, its forces seized control of three airports from federal police.

There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in Amhara, as well as Afar.

Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.

Additional reporting by Peter Mwai, BBC Verify

title: Social worker sues after she says she refused to conceal students’ gender transitions from parents
excerpt:
Albuquerque Public Schools social worker Jeanette Martinez sues her employer over their policy mandating that staff hide a students' gender transition from their parents.

A New Mexico social worker i...
body_text:
Albuquerque Public Schools social worker Jeanette Martinez sues her employer over their policy mandating that staff hide a students' gender transition from their parents.

A New Mexico social worker is suing Albuquerque Public Schools (APS) over a policy she says requires school personnel to conceal students' gender transitions from their parents.

The Center for American Liberty filed a lawsuit in federal court on behalf of Jeanette Martinez, a licensed clinical social worker. Martinez said the district is forcing her to keep parents in the dark regarding their children's social gender transitions, violating her First Amendment rights to free speech and religious freedom.

Martinez, who has worked as a social worker for more than a decade, supports special-education students at Atrisco Heritage Academy High School. Her role requires routine communication with parents regarding academic, behavioral, and special-education needs. As a practicing Christian, Martinez said her deeply held religious convictions prohibit her from lying or intentionally concealing the truth.

BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

School safety programs are collecting students' emails, messages, and web activity on their personal devices. (Sebastian Willnow/picture alliance via Getty Images)

"There was an incident that I was present for where, within two hours, a student verbally decided he was male and wanted to be female," Martinez told Fox News Digital. "Within that meeting, a school team decided right then that because he expressed wanting to be the opposite sex, they would go ahead and choose his new name as the opposite sex."

"They even decided how they were going to introduce his new name to his classmates," Martinez added, noting that school officials also discussed training first-grade students on how to interact with a classmate identifying as the opposite gender.

Under APS Procedural Directive PJ30, staff are instructed to use a student's preferred name and pronouns for internal records, documents and interactions. However, when communicating with parents unless the student or parent has specified otherwise, staff are directed to use the student's legal name and the pronoun corresponding to the student's gender assigned at birth.

FIRST ON FOX: SCHOOL LIED, HID DAUGHTER'S GENDER TRANSITION UNDER DISTRICT POLICY, PARENTS ALLEGE

The Center for American Liberty filed a federal lawsuit Sept. 17 against APS on behalf of Jeanette Martinez, a licensed clinical social worker who alleges that the district is forcing her to conceal students' social gender transitions from their parents in violation of her First Amendment rights. (Getty Images)

The lawsuit alleges that the rule forces employees into a "conspiracy to lie" when parents ask direct questions about their children.

"My job as a social worker is to bring the family together, not to tear them apart," Martinez told Fox News Digital. "To sit there in a parent-teacher conference and try to articulate issues as a mental health provider while participating in that deception is not in the best interest of the student or the family."

In April, Martinez formally requested a religious accommodation that would allow her to communicate truthfully with parents. APS denied the request. According to the lawsuit, Martinez now faces internal investigation, disciplinary action, or potential termination if she refuses to comply with the directive.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

A practicing Christian, Martinez said her faith requires her to tell the truth. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

"It's damaging. It's horrible. It doesn't work. It's unimaginable, to be honest," Martinez said.

Albuquerque Public Schools spokesperson Martin Salazar told Fox News Digital that the district does not comment on pending litigation. However, district guidance notes that the policy is intended to foster a safe learning environment and protect student privacy.

"We will address the allegations in court, using the appropriate process," Salazar said.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

title: Man City found guilty on almost all 115 Premier League charges: Report
excerpt:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges the club has faced regarding breaching Premier League financial rules, according a report in The Athletic.

The sanctions have ...
body_text:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges the club has faced regarding breaching Premier League financial rules, according a report in The Athletic.

The sanctions have not yet been decided, and City are expected to appeal, according to an article by The Athletic’s David Ornstein on Friday, who cited anonymous sources briefed on the matter.

Sanctions could include points deductions, financial penalties, and even stripping titles won by City and relegation from the Premier League.

A spokesperson for City, who have denied the charges, said, “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Since a 2008 takeover by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family, City have been transformed from also-rans into the Premier League’s dominant force.

Eight of the club’s 10 league titles have come in the past 15 seasons, plus a first and only Champions League in 2023.

The club has been accused of breaching financial rules while on the rise to their current status.

Of the 115 charges, 80 are for breaches of regulations from 2009 to 2018, while the remaining 35 relate to failing to cooperate with the Premier League’s investigation.

The charges stem from leaked documents published by the German news magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.

Emails purportedly sent between top City executives showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from the UAE state-controlled airline Etihad and telecommunications firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.

Other documents claimed to show off-the-books payments to then-manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.

City have insisted there is a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” to prove its innocence.

They have already defended their position in one case in which a two-year ban from the Champions League by UEFA was overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in 2020.

The CAS found most of the alleged breaches of overstating sponsorship revenue were either not established or “time-barred” because they fell outside the five-year statutory limit for prosecution.

But no such time limitation clause exists in the Premier League case.

Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.

A severe punishment would also raise doubts about the future of City’s cast of star players, including prolific striker Erling Haaland.

Other clubs could make a claim for titles to be stripped and compensation if City gained an unfair advantage by proscribed means.

title: Pope Leo visits France for first papal visit in 18 years – Europe live
excerpt:
The pope will deliver a landmark speech on AI development and discuss Europe’s future

Pope Leo will visit France this weekend, the first papal state visit to the country in 18 years, beginning with P...
body_text:
The pope will deliver a landmark speech on AI development and discuss Europe’s future

Pope Leo will visit France this weekend, the first papal state visit to the country in 18 years, beginning with Paris today.

During the visit, Leo is expected to seek to repair the Catholic Church’s standing after abuse scandals in the country, as well as deliver a landmark speech on AI development at Unesco and talk about Europe’s future in Metz, with some other European leaders expected to attend.

He will visit the restored Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris, as well as the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, among other places.

The Pope’s plane is now in French airspace and expected to land at Paris Orly airport in the next half hour.

I will keep an eye on his trip and keep you up to date.

Elsewhere, I will bring you all the updates from Ukraine and across the continent.

It’s Friday, 25 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Macron begins with a grand welcome, saying the visit is “a great honour and a source of great joy,” with the pope’s message of hope.

He draws on Pope Leo’s family roots in France, and France’s “unique story that binds Christianity to our nation” over 2,000 years, with the country’s landscape “dotted with cathedrals, basilicas, churches, and priceless monuments.”

He also mentions the reconstruction of the Notre Dame Cathedral, “restored not only for Catholics, but all French people, and indeed, the entire worlds.”

“For Notre-Dame is a part of us, an emblem of that quintessentially French desire to offer the world all the beauty the human spirit can create when moved by an ideal of universal fraternity.”

Macron also says that the French Republic’s secularism is not a “negation of religion,” but an intellectual position that “enables every individual … to think and express their views in all spheres fo life, to believe or not believe.”

He also talks about the growing number of acts of intolerance or hatred against different religions, pledging to protect all places of worship, of all religion.

The president also talks about the need for peace, human rights, sovereignty at a time when all of these get questioned or challenged more often than before.

He also goes through a number of other issues, including the fight against poverty and exclusion, the need for good education, and touches on climate change, too.

Macron also talks about AI, expected to be a big theme of Leo’s visit, as he says “human beings must be liberated by the digital realm, not bound by it.”

“Artificial intelligence must be a servant, not a master. The digital revolution must lead, not enslave. It is therefore our responsibility to prevent the most advanced models from falling into the hands of a few who would then decide for all of humanity. Nor should we allow its most exponential advances to lead us to lose control.”

He also talks about protecting children online, in line with one of his main areas of focus in recent months.

Back to Paris, we are expecting to hear from Macron and Pope Leo shortly.

Meanwhile, Russian authorities released the full results from the country’s parliamentary election, and, would you believe it!?, the main Kremlin party, United Russia, won it big time.

The party will get more than three-fourths of the seats in the lower house, the State Duma, a record high, AP noted. The tightly orchestrated vote excluded virtually any genuine opposition, it added.

“Western governments denounced the polls held in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine as a “sham”.

Russia’s supreme court last month banned the only party that opposes the war, Yabloko, from participating, leaving liberal voters with no option to express discontent.”

And here are some photos from the palace …

Back in Paris, Pope Leo has arrived at the Élysée Palace, where he was greeted by the French president Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte.

Crowds lined the streets of the capital to greet the pope, before his car arrived at the official residency of French president.

A particularly long red carpet was rolled out as the Macrons appeared to warmly welcome Leo to the palace.

Television footage showed the pope and the president talking to one another as they made their way through the grand building.

Ukraine ⁠hit two ⁠Russian ⁠oil refineries in ​the past ⁠day, president Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy ​said.

Zelenskyy ‌said facilities ‌has been struck in Bashkortostan and the ‌Samara region, and ​that there had ⁠also been ​unspecified strikes in ​the ​Black ​Sea.

Meanwhile, we are getting a strong news line from Ukraine, with president Volodymyr Zelenskyy telling reporters that US president Donald Trump told him during their recent meeting that Ukraine would receive licenses for the production of Patriot missiles.

In a voice note to journalists, Zelenskyy said:

“At our last meeting, President Trump emphasised to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licences for the production of Patriot missiles.”

Trump first suggested the move in July, though he later appeared to backtrack on the promise.

As Peter Beaumont explained at the time, it would mark a significant shift for Ukraine – if actually delivered on:

“It would be a diplomatic coup for Kyiv, which has been struggling to counter Moscow’s increasing missile threat.

Zelenskyy has for years been asking for more of [the missiles], and more recently for a license so that Ukraine can manufacture its own. Even at the current increased rate of production it is estimated that the US would not manage to replenish its stockpile for its own use until 2028.”

Leo’s visit in generally secular France attracted a fairly unexpected level of public interest, with over a million people expected to turn out to see him during the four-day trip.

There are a few sticking points between France’s secular public policy and the Catholic church’s teachings, including on abortion (the right was enshrined in the constitution in 2024) and assisted dying. The French Catholic hierarchy opposed both measures, but Leo is seen as unlikely to wade into these issues.

In political terms, the pope’s visit is seen as a big win for Macron in his final months in the office: his predecessor, Pope Francis, visited France three times, but never on an official state visit.

Only around 5% of France’s 69 million residents regularly attend Catholic church, AFP noted, but some 40% see themselves as Catholic.

Interestingly, Leo’s paternal ancestors were French, so there’s also that.

Later today, Pope Leo will go to the Élysée Palace for (another) formal welcome and a meeting with authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps, before visiting Unesco and delivering a speech on AI in mid-afternoon.

He is then expected to go on a stroll through the streets of Paris, before going to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral.

In the evening, he is due to meet with some 80,000 young people for a prayer vigil with young people at Stade de France (I decline to say what they consider as ‘young’, because I’m not happy their brackets.)

Tomorrow, he will visit Maison Bakhita social support and integration centre and hold a meeting at the Catholic Institute of Paris before hosting an open-air mass at Place de la Concorde and Avenue des Champs-Elysees and moving onwards to Lourdes.

He will spend all Sunday there, with a Sunday Mass in the Sanctuary of Lourdes, and a private meeting with victims of sexual abuse within the Church later that day.

He will then be in Metz on Monday, with a speech on the roots of united Europe, another stroll through the streets of the city, and a mass at Metz Cathedral, before flying back to Rome.

Pope Leo gets off the plane, gets into a chat with Macron, and so the official welcome ceremony begins.

The plane is now in sight, and president Macron in position to welcome the pope to France.

Meanwhile, frantic preparations are under way at the Élysée Palace, where the pope is expected later this morning…

But first, back to Orly airport in Paris.

To welcome Pope Leo to France, the bells of churches across France started ringing at 10am, just as his plane touched down at Paris Orly.

In fact, they are still ringing: it was agreed they would ring for seven minutes, which the Conference of Bishops of France said would be just right to “mark the solemnity of the event without disrupting civil life.”

It’s seen as “a symbolic gesture to mark the beginning of this apostolic journey and allow everyone to join in, wherever they are.”

Meanwhile, AP is reporting that in what will surely be seen as a swipe at Donald Trump, Pope Leo told reporters on board of his plane that they are always welcome to cover him, and affirmed the need for media scrutiny.

These comments came in response to a question about Trump ban at the White House, AP is reporting.

As I was chatting about politics, Pope Leo’s plane has just landed in Paris.

Last night Macron gave a rare prime time TV interview, answering questions about all sorts of current issues.

Talking to TF1 and France2, he denied media reports from Spain that the US Central Intelligence Agency warned Paris of a potential Russian strike across southern Europe, from the Mediterranean (Europe Live, Thursday).

“I can deny ‌it. The CIA did not inform French services,” he said.

But he still repeated his warning about Russia’s “growing” hostile activities in Europe, saying all sensitive sites in France are subject to additional protection.

The French president also said that said any ban on US diesel exports backed by president Donald Trump would be a “bad” decision, including for the US economy.

Interestingly, French president Emmanuel Macron will meet with Pope Leo this morning and host him at the Élysée Palace, but will not attend tomorrow’s mass at Place de la Concorde in Paris.

Former president Nicolas Sarkozy said the decision was Macron’s personal choice, adding that he would have attended if he were still in office.

“Some say that in the name of secularism, he shouldn’t go. That doesn’t make sense: secularism is a right, a right to believe or not to believe,” he said, quoted by BFM TV.

French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu will represent the state on Saturday instead.

Pope Leo will visit France this weekend, the first papal state visit to the country in 18 years, beginning with Paris today.

During the visit, Leo is expected to seek to repair the Catholic Church’s standing after abuse scandals in the country, as well as deliver a landmark speech on AI development at Unesco and talk about Europe’s future in Metz, with some other European leaders expected to attend.

He will visit the restored Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris, as well as the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, among other places.

The Pope’s plane is now in French airspace and expected to land at Paris Orly airport in the next half hour.

I will keep an eye on his trip and keep you up to date.

Elsewhere, I will bring you all the updates from Ukraine and across the continent.

It’s Friday, 25 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: Polanski heckled at Jewish community hustings after saying that Zionism is a form of racism – UK politics live
excerpt:
The Green leader, who is Jewish, made the remarks as part of his campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics live blog.

Zack Polanski declared himself a...
body_text:
The Green leader, who is Jewish, made the remarks as part of his campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics live blog.

Zack Polanski declared himself an anti-Zionist and faced heckling at a Jewish community hustings in Holborn and St Pancras, where the Green party leader is standing as a candidate in next month’s byelection.

He said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – was a form of racism because it involved the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. His remarks were met with boos from the audience last night.

“I’m an anti-Zionist. I think countries have always been ideas and I think things change over time,” he said.

Polanski, who is Jewish, said criticising the Israeli government and the occupation of Palestinian land was not antisemitic. “We need to come together to recognise that when we call that antisemitic, we are making ourselves as Jewish people less safe,” he added.

As the Green party prepares for its annual conference, members are due to vote on a motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism in official policy. As my colleague Peter Walker reported last week, some in the party fear it could alienate Jewish supporters if it passed:

double quotation markA Green official said that many activists loyal to the party’s leadership might not be at the autumn conference because it takes place a week before voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which Polanski hopes to take Keir Starmer’s old seat from Labour, potentially leaving more scope for others to push through the motion.

“The risk is that if it passes as it is we are alienating ourselves from the Jewish community in the UK, a lot of whom are not big fans of the current Israeli government,” a Green source said.

There was, they added, a parallel worry about internal splits, with some Green activists in leaked WhatsApp chats warning that Polanski was “struggling to overcome Zionist indoctrination”.

Zack Polanski is reportedly backing two amendments that would tone down the ‘Zionism is racism’ motion, according to Sky News.

As reported by the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker, the motion calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants”, and says the Palestinian people have the full right to “resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” within international law.

If passed, Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism” by the party, it adds.

Sky News reported that the amendments, which have been selected for a vote at the Green party conference next week, “pushback on the call for a single Palestinian state with Jerusalem as its capital, and add safeguards for Jewish members who are part of groups that describe themselves as Zionist”.

Foreign secretary Ed Miliband told his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Britain will “not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil”. The comments were made during a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York, Foreign Office said. The pair discussed the war in the Middle East, the strait of Hormuz crisis and the UK’s “unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil”, according to a readout of the meeting.

Advisers in No 10 are pushing for the prime minister to call an early election as part of an attempt to keep Labour in power, according to the Telegraph. The newspaper reported senior members of Andy Burnham’s team believe calling an election in spring would give the party the best chance of winning another majority.

Defence companies and critical infrastructure providers will be briefed on the threat posed by Russia and its proxies, including cyber attacks, sabotage and disinformation targeting organisations vital to Ukraine’s defence. The government announced security minister Dan Jarvis and Armed Forces minister Louise Sandher-Jones will chair closed-door meetings with industry leaders in the coming weeks.
