title: Israel moves to bar both main Arab lists from October election
excerpt: Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to bar both main Arab electoral lists from next month’s election, putting the political representation of Palestinian citizens of Israel before the Supre...
body_text:
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to bar both main Arab electoral lists from next month’s election, putting the political representation of Palestinian citizens of Israel before the Supreme Court weeks before voters go to the polls.

The committee voted on Wednesday to disqualify the United Arab List, or Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, and the Joint List, an alliance of the Arab-led Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties. It also voted separately to bar Hadash legislator Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh. The election is scheduled for October 27.

The bans are not final. Decisions against individual candidates require Supreme Court approval, while lists can appeal their exclusion. Adalah, the legal centre representing the parties and candidates, says it will challenge the votes when the court hears the cases next week.

Ra’am called its exclusion “political and unacceptable”, saying the decision was intended to prevent it from influencing the balance of power and changing the government.

The Joint List said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir were trying to discourage Arab citizens from voting “because they fear our ability to bring down the government of genocide and racism”. Its leader, Yousef Jabareen, questioned how the committee could bar parties representing more than 1.25 million voters.

Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that his exclusion was an attempt to silence criticism of government policy and said the decisions would be challenged in court and through public protest. Rejecting the allegation that he supports violence, he told The Times of Israel: “I have never called for violence or terrorism. I oppose armed struggle.”

The petitions invoke Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, which allows a list or candidate to be excluded for denying Israel’s existence as a “Jewish and democratic state”, inciting racism or supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or an organisation designated as terrorist.

Netanyahu’s Likud party sought to disqualify the Joint List and Cassif, and was among the groups that filed against Ra’am. Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party also sought to bar Abu Shehadeh. Adalah disputes the allegations. It says the case against Ra’am presents no evidence that the party supports armed struggle, while the Joint List petition relies heavily on old material, including bills proposed in previous Knessets.

Abu Shehadeh’s case has drawn a different response. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara found no legal basis to exclude the other targeted parties and candidates but said an article he published on October 8, 2023, which she said may constitute support for armed struggle, warranted serious examination. The committee voted 31-4 to bar him. Adalah says the article contains no such call.

The push to bar Abu Shehadeh drew support from parties outside Netanyahu’s coalition. According to The Times of Israel, opposition parties voted to disqualify him, as did Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, who chairs the elections committee. The vote broke with decades of precedent in which committee chairs abstained from disqualification votes. Abu Shehadeh’s exclusion still requires approval from the full Supreme Court.

Ra’am joined the coalition government formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in 2021, helping end Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office in 2021, although Abbas had previously discussed cooperation with Netanyahu as well. Now Likud itself has filed petitions against Arab representation, while Ben-Gvir’s party has pursued separate exclusions.

A Channel 12 poll published on Tuesday projected seven seats for the Joint List and five for Ra’am, against 50 for Netanyahu’s current coalition bloc. The 12 projected Arab seats would not automatically back Netanyahu’s opponents, as mainstream opposition parties remain divided over whether to govern with Arab support. But removing both lists would change the possible routes to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.

The Supreme Court has overturned previous committee bans on Arab lists and candidates, including Balad’s exclusion in 2022. It must now decide whether the evidence meets the legal threshold for barring the two principal lists seeking to represent Palestinian citizens of Israel. The ruling will determine who can appear on the October ballot.

title: Beau Lamarre-Condon sized up surfboard bag against friend before allegedly murdering Sydney couple, court told
excerpt:
Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies before concealing bodies in bags purchased from sports store

Beau Lamarre-Condon was seen sizing up a surfboa...
body_text:
Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies before concealing bodies in bags purchased from sports store

Beau Lamarre-Condon was seen sizing up a surfboard bag used to dispose of a victim days before the police officer murdered two men, prosectors have alleged in a Sydney court, with chilling CCTV footage shown to the jury.

Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, with his police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The 31-year-old earlier this week pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

CCTV footage taken from Miranda Westfield on 17 February was played to the NSW supreme court trial on Thursday showing Lamarre-Condon’s movements before the alleged murders.

In the compilation, Lamarre-Condon’s grey Tesla is seen passing by the shopping centre before the police officer and a friend enter a Decathlon store.

The pair walk straight to the surfboard bag section, where Lamarre-Condon runs his hands across the options before picking out a cover.

He holds it up and appears to measure it against his friend’s height as the other man stands straight. The bag clears his friend’s head by a few centimetres.

Watching from the pews of the Sydney courtroom, Davies and Baird’s family shook their heads as the footage was played.

During the prosecution’s openings on Monday, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC alleged Lamarre-Condon asked his friend whether he would fit in the bag.

In the footage, Lamarre-Condon takes the bag to the cashier and pays for it using $90 in cash, according to receipts shown to the court.

Two days later, the police officer would allegedly shoot the two men and place Baird in the bag purchased from the Westfield, the prosecution alleged.

Lamarre-Condon returned to the same store shortly after the shooting to buy a second surfboard bag to conceal Davies’ body, Hatfield told the court.

The defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.

The prosecution has told the jury that Lamarre-Condon developed an “infatuation and obsession” with Baird after their brief relationship that manifested in compulsive behaviour which escalated. It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.

The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

title: Venezuela’s Delcy Rodriguez promises elections at UN, gives no date
excerpt: Venezuela’s acting president told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday that the country would hold elections as part of a transition to “full democracy”, but did not give a specific...
body_text:
Venezuela’s acting president told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday that the country would hold elections as part of a transition to “full democracy”, but did not give a specific date for the vote.

“I wish to state this very clearly before this General Assembly: Elections will be held in Venezuela,” Delcy Rodriguez said, adding that her government has started a “political dialogue with opposition sectors” to secure a “process based on equal conditions for all.”

Rodriguez said that the Venezuelan people will determine the best time to get elections moving and assured the UN that, when the time comes, the country’s institutions “will be prepared to guarantee an inclusive and transparent process”.

Rodriguez took over as Venezuela’s interim president after a surprise United States military raid in January that abducted then-leader Nicolas Maduro and brought him to the US to face drug trafficking charges.

This is the first trip to the US by a Venezuelan head of state since 2018, when Maduro travelled to New York to participate in the UNGA. He is currently being held only a few miles from the organisation’s headquarters as he awaits trial.

Rodriguez’s participation in the international forum also marks a milestone in Venezuela’s reintegration into global diplomacy. She faced a delicate balance in her closely watched UN speech, which needed to be addressed to both her people and the US government that holds her predecessor.

She said her country is coming back strong after “setbacks” suffered this year and thanked US President Donald Trump for being willing to resume relations after the US military spirited her predecessor out of the country.

Rodriguez met with Trump briefly on the sidelines of the assembly on Tuesday. Among other matters, Trump and Rodriguez discussed restructuring the South American nation’s billions of dollars in sovereign debt.

Critics say Washington has sidelined the Venezuelan opposition, dropping demands for free elections in favour of oil and investment deals with the interim government.

“Today, Venezuela is being reborn,” Rodriguez said in her remarks to the international forum.

“I do not promise you an easy way forward,” Rodriguez said, saying she was addressing her people. “Rebuilding our national soul will be the priority.”

title: Turkiye agrees to gradual handover of Bashiqa base to Iraq
excerpt:
Turkiye and Iraq have agreed to a gradual transfer of Ankara’s military base in Bashiqa to Baghdad, according to a statement released by the Iraqi prime minister’s office.

The announcement followed a...
body_text:
Turkiye and Iraq have agreed to a gradual transfer of Ankara’s military base in Bashiqa to Baghdad, according to a statement released by the Iraqi prime minister’s office.

The announcement followed a meeting on Wednesday between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

“Within this framework, they reached an agreement on fully establishing state authority in Sinjar and ending the presence of outlawed foreign armed elements,” Iraq’s prime minister’s office announced, in an apparent reference to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), which has maintained a presence in the mountainous Sinjar region of northern Iraq.

“The two sides also agreed to expand the volume of bilateral trade and investment, to implement signed agreements immediately, and to accelerate joint strategic projects, particularly the Development Road project,” the office added.

The decision to transfer the facility addresses a longstanding flashpoint between the two neighbours.

Turkiye first established the base in Bashiqa, northeast of Mosul, in December 2015 through an agreement with the autonomous Kurdistan Regional Government to train local forces fighting the ISIL (ISIS) group.

The deployment of up to 600 Turkish soldiers drew criticism from Baghdad, which viewed the presence as a violation of Iraqi sovereignty.

The Sinjar region has long been a focal point for Turkish military operations targeting fighters from the PKK.

Cross-border operations in Sinjar had eased following a landmark peace process between Ankara and the PKK in 2025, paving the way for federal authorities to assert control over the border zone.

Wednesday’s accord caps months of efforts by Baghdad to consolidate state authority over northern flashpoints, while aligning with Ankara on trade corridors and security coordination along their shared frontier.

title: Michigan student confronts El-Sayed over Iran stance in tense exchange: ‘Do you stand with us?’
excerpt:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is pressed by a student at a town hall over Iran and his past comments on Ali Khamenei.

A Michigan student confronted Democratic U.S. Senate candid...
body_text:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is pressed by a student at a town hall over Iran and his past comments on Ali Khamenei.

A Michigan student confronted Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his position on Iran during a town hall Wednesday, invoking his family's stated persecution by the Iranian regime before repeatedly pressing the candidate to say whether he stood with Iranians opposing the government.

Iman Dashti, who identified himself as Persian, told El-Sayed during a town hall at the University of Michigan that members of his family had suffered under Iran's government.

"My cousin was hunted in the streets of Iran by the IRGC because her hijab wasn't on right," Dashti said. He also alleged that her uncle had been sentenced to death and received 50 lashes under the Iranian government.

ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS

US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan Abdul El-Sayed speaks with reporters during a Student Meet and Greet at the Michigan Theatre in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on August 26, 2026. (JEFF KOWALSKY / AFP via Getty Images)

Dashti then confronted El-Sayed over leaked audio from earlier this year in which he said he did not want to comment on the death of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei because "there are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today."

"That silence had a gaping hole in our community," Dashti told El-Sayed Wednesday.

He asked whether he regretted that silence, whether he would renounce people who held vigils supporting Khamenei and whether he stood "unequivocally against the IRGC" and the Islamic Republic of Iran.

El-Sayed responded by arguing that the United States has too often acted as "the world's policeman" while saying he supported movements for democracy and freedom abroad.

AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"One can disagree with the governance of a foreign country. One can stand in solidarity with freedom and democracy movements," El-Sayed said.

He went on to reject U.S.-led regime change in Iran.

"I will always stand for and with democratic movements always," El-Sayed said. "But I also don't believe that we were in the right to go to war to topple the government of Iran. It was not our responsibility to do. It is the responsibility of the people of Iran to decide what their leadership should look like."

Dashti pressed him again. "You stand with us?" he asked.

"I will always stand with movements for freedom and democracy," El-Sayed responded, before again warning against U.S. involvement in regime change.

"We should not be in the business of regime change," he said.

El-Sayed added moments later, "I want freedom and democracy for the people of Iran, no question. But I want that to be done by the people of Iran, coming together as a community to decide how to create democratic change in their society."

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for additional comment on the exchange and attempted to reach Dashti through Instagram.

El-Sayed, who won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in August, is running against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The contest has drawn substantial national attention and spending.

The Iran confrontation was one of several notable exchanges during Wednesday's "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall at El-Sayed's alma mater.

KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN

Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during the Michigan Democratic Party's 2026 nominating convention in Lansing, Michigan, US, on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While discussing public health infrastructure, El-Sayed appeared to make a prediction about the party and the gender that will win the White House in 2028.

"I'm looking forward to working with the next Democratic president when she takes office in 2029," El-Sayed said, adding that he hoped to work with that administration to modernize the nation's public health infrastructure.

El-Sayed did not identify whom he had in mind.

His remarks came as former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democrat presidential nominee, returned to Michigan to campaign with El-Sayed. Harris has not announced a 2028 presidential campaign.

El-Sayed also criticized President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance during the event.

"Donald Trump and JD Vance can't seem to keep my name out their mouth," El-Sayed said. "They don't really know how to say it, though, which is fine, because I believe in teaching opportunities."

Trump and other national Republicans have repeatedly targeted El-Sayed during the midterm campaign, while El-Sayed has responded by criticizing the president.

"As he noted in his response, Abdul will always stand with movements for freedom and democracy and he condemns government anti-free speech violence," Roxie Richner, El-Sayed campaign spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Abdul has also been clear that the United States should not be in the business of spending our tax dollars abroad on regime change wars that take our servicemembers’ lives, waste our tax dollars, and raise our prices. He believes American taxpayer dollars are best spent here at home to invest in infrastructure, education, and healthcare."

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?
excerpt:
When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.

There have been multiple reports of the ...
body_text:
When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.

There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage.

The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK,  JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them.

On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy.

To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy.

Mark Zuckerberg - who wore a set at an event in California last year - predicts that smart glasses will replace mobile phones

The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life.

When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause.

"We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully.

Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away?

Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media?

There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial.

I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street.

The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe.

That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded.

The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you.

My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera.

Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer.  I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand.

Left: Meta's demonstration of a user making a phone call, with an image of the person they're talking to displayed inside their glasses. Right: Zoe Kleinman wearing a set on her commute

And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data.

When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life.

My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog.

Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it).

More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland.

The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart.

Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year.

Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of smart glasses, is furious.

"They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes."

Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population.

"We don't need them, we don't want them," she says.

Tech founder Liz Hunter is campaigning for tighter regulation of smart glasses

A Polish developer has released an app called ZuckOff which uses Bluetooth to identify nearby smart glasses. It's been downloaded thousands of times, reports Wired magazine.

Ben Wood, from tech research firm CCS Insight, remembers first reading the phrase "pervert glasses" in the usually strait-laced Financial Times - a sign, he says, that it had prompted a "significant public backlash".

The furore has not deterred other companies from eyeing the market, however.

Samsung is reported to be working on a collaboration with the upmarket glasses brand Warby Parker. Google is also said to be working on a set. Snap, the firm behind Snapchat, has just launched Specs, which are retailing in the US for $2,195 (and £1,995 in the UK). Users can see data inside the glass, and snap their fingers to take a photo.

Snap founder Evan Spiegel says he thinks smart glasses will eventually replace phones, and he's not alone.

When Meta launched smart glasses in 2021, they were geared in part around what the user could see. The firm promised they would allow users to "easily record the world as you see it", and to "capture life's moments as they happen from a unique first-person perspective".

So Meta's latest announcement - glasses without a camera - is notable.

Janusz Swierczynski, a researcher at Oxford University's Saïd Business School, who is worried about smart glasses, says the release of a camera-free version is a "positive sign" that Meta seems to have listened to privacy concerns. "They're thinking about it and that they're responding," he says, though he thinks it's "not a perfect" response because the camera-enabled glasses are still on the market.

Others are less sure it represents a real shift.

"It's certainly not the end of cameras in glasses," says Wood, from CCS Insight. He thinks that smart glasses are largely about capturing information; the glasses collect as much data as they can from your surroundings and then use AI to tell you about it.

And glasses armed with a camera - trained on whatever you can see - are an "extremely good" source of that information.

"That is an invaluable data stream to an AI platform, which can then interpret that data and provide you with the best possible information related to it," Wood says. "So having the vision parts of it with the cameras is a key pillar for getting the best experience."

How the social media ban could reshape how all of us use the internet

AI 'slop' is transforming social media - and a backlash is brewing

Tech billionaires seem to be doom prepping. Should we all be worried?

He imagines Meta has been working on the camera-free glasses for several years, and the current backlash over privacy provides "fantastic timing" for their release.

Indeed, Meta doesn't yet show any signs of slowing down its development of camera-enabled glasses. The company is bringing its third generation of the glasses to the UK next month. These can visually display data inside the specs' lenses. (As a live broadcast journalist who has talked openly about brain fog, I can see the appeal of glasses that can discreetly display a script).

Kate Winick, a tech analyst at the research firm Forrester, says it's not a step back from camera-enabled glasses but more of a "half step to the side, where they give users time to get comfortable with the technology… so that users themselves start to say, 'Oh, this would be so much more useful if it had a camera'."

And she says, paradoxically, the existence of camera-free glasses might help "take the heat" off people who wear camera-enabled glasses in public. "It's now clear that out in the market some glasses have cameras and some don't," she says. "You can't automatically get mad at everybody wearing Meta's glasses, because you may not know whether or not they have a camera."

And other companies are trying to address privacy concerns in different ways - without getting rid of the camera.

The Taiwanese firm HTC recently launched Vive Eagle glasses, which cost less than a quarter of Snap's.

Thomas Dexmier, a vice president at HTC Vive, says that if anyone near an Eagle specs wearer says "stop filming" or "stop recording", and it is picked up by one of the four microphones, the camera will deactivate.

And he adds that all recordings captured by the glasses are encrypted, and the firm itself cannot see them -  though this also means HTC cannot flag harmful content.

"We acknowledge that there are some challenges, potentially becoming a real problem, especially for women," he said.

He said HTC Vive was working to make it as difficult as possible for the tech to be misused but said it was "too early to comment" on whether the firm would consider a version without cameras.

Ultimately, Wood thinks that camera-enabled glasses are "not going away".

He says the current moment reminds him of the 2000s, when some people said that mobile phone companies couldn't install cameras in their devices because of similar concerns over privacy. "There's an inevitability there," he says.

"We will have to find a societal norm, a framework for the use of these products."

BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. title: NYC kitten rescue defends ‘NO F---ING MAGA’ adoption policy as PETA calls for it to be abolished
excerpt:
'My View with Lara Trump' spotlights 'Paws of War,' an organization that rescues cats and dogs and pairs them with veterans, first responders and their families.

After posting an explicit warning tha...
body_text:
'My View with Lara Trump' spotlights 'Paws of War,' an organization that rescues cats and dogs and pairs them with veterans, first responders and their families.

After posting an explicit warning that MAGA supporters, conservatives, and apolitical applicants need not apply, a New York City kitten rescue is defending its screening process against mounting criticism — including from PETA, which called on the group to scrap the ideological ban.

"Homeless animals don’t care which side of abortion you are on or whether you believe in global warming or support Palestine or Israel, or if you don’t vote at all, ever: they care if you love them and will give them a good home," PETA founder Ingrid Newkirk told Fox News Digital.

"We hope this policy, which is humancentric, is reconsidered and abolished," Newkirk said.

The dispute centers on Itty Bitty City Kitties, a Rockaway Beach-based rescue that describes itself as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit specializing in orphaned and neonatal kittens, feral-cat welfare and adoptions. The organization is also listed among New York state’s registered pet rescues.

ONE OF NATION'S LARGEST CHRISTIAN FOSTER AGENCIES WILL NOT ALLOW LGBTQ COUPLES TO ADOPT CHILDREN

In an email from Itty Bitty City Kitties to Fox News Digital, director Samantha Knox said, "Active support for or alignment with social movements that normalize, celebrate, or promote systemic cruelty, human suffering, forced family separation, or the abandonment of animals during forced family displacements, is not treated as a theoretical opinion." (Getty Images)

In a social media post reviewed by Fox News Digital, the rescue laid out a series of political positions it said could disqualify prospective adopters.

"‘I’m not political’? Nice loophole. Still nope."

An accompanying image of a kitten bore the message, "NO. F---ING. MAGA."

The post drew wider attention after Libs of TikTok posted it on X, prompting questions about whether the language represented the rescue’s actual adoption practices.

Fox News Digital contacted Itty Bitty City Kitties and asked whether an applicant could be rejected for identifying as MAGA, conservative or apolitical.

Samantha Knox, who has publicly identified herself as the director of Itty Bitty City Kitties, defended the organization’s screening approach by saying its overriding responsibility is the welfare of the animals in its care.

"As an animal welfare rescue, our primary responsibility is ensuring the animals in our care go to safe, compassionate homes," Knox told Fox News Digital.

She said the organization considers "public conduct and demonstrated values" and argued that a record of "celebrat[ing] cruelty" can raise concerns about an applicant’s suitability to care for an animal.

"A history of celebrating harm or abuse, be it toward people or animals, is one of the biggest red flags in animal rescue," Knox said. "We stand by our mission and will never place a vulnerable animal with anyone, ever, who we feel is a danger to the welfare of the animal."

OREGON SETTLES WITH CHRISTIAN MOTHER DENIED FOSTER CARE ADOPTION OVER GENDER IDENTITY BELIEFS

Itty Bitty City Kitties posted to its Facebook page, saying, "MAGA? Nope. Conservative? Nope." (Getty Images)

Fox News Digital followed up with a narrower question, asking whether a person who identifies as MAGA or conservative, but has no documented history of animal cruelty, threats, neglect or violence, would be eligible to adopt.

"Itty Bitty City Kitties does not screen or reject applicants based on registered political party affiliation," Knox responded. "MAGA is a political movement and ideology, not a recognized political party."

Knox said adoption evaluations instead concern "conduct, ethical alignment, and animal safety."

"We reserve the right to reject any application where an applicant’s expressed values, public statements, or actions demonstrate a failure to meet our safety and welfare standards," she said.

NEW JERSEY POLICE PULL OUT 3-FOOT PYTHON FROM WOMAN'S CAR GRILLE, BODYCAM VIDEO SHOWS

Asked again whether a MAGA or conservative applicant without a history of cruelty, threats, neglect or violence could adopt from the organization, Knox did not provide a yes-or-no answer.

"Media-driven requests to force complex animal welfare evaluations into a binary ‘yes or no’ premise fundamentally misrepresent how responsible adoption screenings operate," she said.

Knox added that "active support for or alignment with social movements" the rescue believes normalizes or promotes cruelty can be treated as "actionable conduct," and said adoption decisions are made "holistically under these welfare and safety standards."

Knox also provided Fox News Digital with screenshots she said showed explicit, hostile messages directed at the rescue following its political posts.

Knox said messages of that nature illustrated the kind of conduct the rescue considers relevant when evaluating prospective homes. PETA, however, drew a different line.

"Political affiliation is not a reliable measure of whether someone will be a good guardian," the organization told Fox News Digital, while adding that a person's actions, statements, along with demonstrated treatment of people and animals, can be relevant to an adoption decision.

PETA has supported cutting taxpayer funding for animal testing following President Donald Trump's return to the White House. (Adam J. Dewey/Anadolu via Getty Images)

PETA said rescues should focus on "objective animal-welfare factors," including an applicant’s history of animal care, ability to meet an animal’s needs and evidence of cruelty, neglect or violence. "Shelters and rescues exist to protect animals, not to serve as political gatekeepers," PETA said.

Itty Bitty City Kitties’ public adoption page describes what the organization calls a "Fully Supported Adoption Model," under which prospective owners submit an application, provide references, employment and living information, participate in a phone interview and complete a FaceTime or Zoom interview in lieu of a home visit.

The rescue’s published "MUST LIST" says adopters must keep animals up to date on veterinary care, keep them indoors or leashed outside, never declaw them, maintain a plan for travel, illness or death, not simply give away an animal they can no longer care for, and be financially able to provide for its welfare.

The public-facing requirements reviewed by Fox News Digital do not mention MAGA, conservatism, political affiliation or political ideology.

The organization has also used its social media account for other political messaging.

On Sept. 10, Itty Bitty City Kitties posted an image of a kitten carrying the words, "Kittens. Don’t. Mourn. Nazis."

"For absolutely no reason at all on this day one year later..." text on the image stated. "Just a little kitten making sure we all know where we stand," the accompanying caption read, followed by hashtags including "#kitten," "#cat," "#politics" and "#iykyk."

While the post did not name late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, it was published exactly one year after his assassination at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025.

Knox also invoked the rescue’s nonprofit status in defending its ability to take positions on political and social issues, saying 501(c)(3) organizations are permitted to maintain issue-based standards aligned with their missions, as long as they do not engage in partisan political campaigning.

PETA, while objecting to the use of political affiliation as a measure of adoption suitability, said an applicant’s actual behavior toward animals can, and should, matter regardless of ideology.

"More broadly, anyone who condones, celebrates, or participates in harming animals demonstrates a troubling lack of empathy," PETA said.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: In historic first, tropical turtles spotted nesting on California beaches
excerpt:
What caused the turtles to begin nesting farther north than usual is the ‘million dollar question’

A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last weekend around sunset and started l...
body_text:
What caused the turtles to begin nesting farther north than usual is the ‘million dollar question’

A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last weekend around sunset and started laying eggs in the sand.

People on Huntington Beach who saw the female olive ridley sea turtle were shocked and excited. And they weren’t the only ones freaking out, said Justin Viezbicke, the California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (Noaa).

“This is the first documented case of a turtle nesting on the west coast,” Viezbicke said.

What made the sighting even more noteworthy is that two different olive ridley sea turtles were identified laying eggs on Orange county beaches in the last week, the first on Seal Beach and the second on Huntington Beach. It’s a pattern that has scientists questioning whether the nestings are a freak occurrence, or the beginnings of a more lasting trend.

While early news reports suggested that a single female turtle laid eggs on both California beaches, scientists further analyzed photographs of the turtles’ shell shape and barnacle patterns and determined that two separate olive ridley turtles had begun nesting on the US coast, Viezbicke said.

Olive ridley turtles typically lay their eggs on beaches much further to the south, in Mexico and Central America, Viezbicke said.

What caused the turtles to begin nesting further north than usual is the “million dollar question”, he said. Scientists are examining several different theories, including the environmental factor of warmer coastal waters, to other effects of El Niño, or whether the turtles “could have been blown off course by the recent hurricane”.

“There’s been a lot of activity in the Pacific Ocean,” Viezbicke said.

While it’s too soon to tell, it’s also possible that these first recorded US coastal nests could herald a broader northward shift in the olive ridley turtle’s nesting patterns, one driven by climate crisis and the warming ocean waters in the turtles’ native nesting areas, said Lance Adams, an aquarium veterinarian at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.

The sex of the olive ridley turtle is determined by temperatures where the eggs hatch, and warmer temperatures produce more female turtles. “After about 87.8F, they’re almost all female,” Adams said. To achieve a balanced population, the sea turtles might need access to cooler nesting areas.

On the other hand, it’s hard to generalize from just two sightings, Adams said: “The turtles could be here by mistake.”

Because the nesting season is not over and individual olive ridley turtles typically lay multiple nests of eggs, “We might see additional sea turtles making beach crawls to nest in the next 30 to 90 days,” Adams said.

For protection, the new turtle nests have been surrounded by fencing. But there’s only so much local officials can do to protect the eggs, which typically take 45 to 60 days to hatch, Viezbicke said.

It’s not just the dangers from local predators, such as coyotes, or from interfering humans. New hurricane swells and high tides are expected as soon as Monday of next week, Viezbicke said – and there’s a risk of the extreme weather “washing away that part of the beach”.

Californians who spot sea turtles on a local beach should not interfere with them, and should keep at least 50 ft away, Adams, the aquarium veterinarian, advised. To advise authorities of a new turtle sighting, tell a lifeguard, or call Noaa’s marine animal stranding hotline, he recommended.

Getting close to the turtles’ fenced-off nesting spots is not a good idea, he said: “People won’t see anything.” If locals want to observe live sea turtles in action, they can visit rescued turtles on display in rehabilitation tanks at an aquarium.

Olive ridley sea turtles are one of the most abundant turtle species worldwide, but are protected under the US endangered species act.

Warmer ocean temperatures have led to sightings of all kinds of sea creatures that aren’t typically spotted on the California coast, he noted, including different shark species, rays, sea horses and the venomous yellow-bellied sea snake.

People should aim to adapt to shift in wildlife patterns, and, in general, keep their distance, Adams said, though new unexpected species present different potential risks.

“Turtles aren’t particularly dangerous to humans. They can bite. They can slap with their flippers. Someone could potentially get hurt, but probably not seriously,” he said.

title: English soccer star Harry Kane wants to play in the MLS and kick in the NFL at the same time
excerpt:
Sports Talk takes a shocking turn when a caller informs Cal that he is the latest recipient of the Nobel Prize.

We don't see enough two-sport athletes these days. It's such a cool phenomenon that we ...
body_text:
Sports Talk takes a shocking turn when a caller informs Cal that he is the latest recipient of the Nobel Prize.

We don't see enough two-sport athletes these days. It's such a cool phenomenon that we haven't really seen in a while.

However, English soccer star Harry Kane wouldn't mind taking a crack at it.

Because if he winds up in the MLS, he wouldn't mind spending his free time on an NFL roster.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

England's Harry Kane celebrates after scoring on a penalty kick during a World Cup round of 16 soccer match against Mexico in Mexico City on Sunday, July 5, 2026. (Eduardo Verdugo/AP)

ENGLISH SOCCER STAR HARRY KANE CALLS ROUND OF GOLF WITH TRUMP A ‘SURREAL EXPERIENCE’

According to The Athletic, Kane was recently quoted as saying that he was close to re-upping with the Bundesliga's Bayern Munich. That led to a question about his plans beyond this next deal.

One of those plans was something he has reportedly talked about multiple times over the years, and that was switching sports.

He's talked about golfing professionally, but this time he was focused on trading football for American football.

"That is something I will try and look at a bit more seriously," he said. "It all depends on what happens in my career over the next five or six years, the motivation and what I want to do. The NFL is a lot more realistic than the golf one, let’s put it that way."

But what had never come up before was the idea of Kane winding down his career stateside in the MLS while also moonlighting as a placekicker.

SOMEONE NEEDS TO STEP IN AND DEFEND CODY RHODES' AWFUL, TERRIBLE PLACEKICKING PERFORMANCE

England's Harry Kane checks out of the game during a World Cup round of 16 soccer match between Mexico and England in Mexico City, Sunday, July 5, 2026. (Ricardo Mazalan/AP Photo)

"Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that it might be a thing where you could connect the two, with the seasons," he said. "But it is in the back of my mind because right now, I am feeling that I want to play as long as I can here."

Nice save at the end. The team about to re-sign you probably doesn't want to hear about your plans to play in the MLS and kick extra points on the side.

But do you know who does want to hear that? The rest of us.

That would just be a fun thing to watch, and Kane obviously has the leg to boot a pigskin quite a long way if he can nail down those pesky mechanics.

Which it looks like he may have already done.

At least a few teams are probably setting reminders to see what Kane is up to when his Bayern Munich deal is up.

Maybe it's a pipe dream, but someone has to bring back two-sport professional athletes.

title: Risking their lives to find food and water in Russian-occupied city
excerpt:
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped

"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.

She is trapped in the Russ...
body_text:
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped

"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.

She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.

Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.

They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.

They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.

Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.

Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.

Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.

It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.

Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.

Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.

Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city

Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.

The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.

Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023.

Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive.

"There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May.

"I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."

Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.

Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions

Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.

No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.

While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.

These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year

Warning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.

Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult.

The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.

Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.

Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.

She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information.

"I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."

While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.

Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety.

"They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.

Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says

A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents

Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station

Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.

They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana.

Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is  not possible in Oleshky.

Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".

Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".

That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish.

"This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.

"If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.

Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone

title: Just one small serving of ultra-processed food a day linked to higher disease risk, major study finds
excerpt: New York-based registered dietitian Kelly Springer shares research on highly processed foods and explains how combining fruits, vegetables, nuts and other nutrient-rich options can support long-term h...
body_text:
New York-based registered dietitian Kelly Springer shares research on highly processed foods and explains how combining fruits, vegetables, nuts and other nutrient-rich options can support long-term health.

Just an extra 3.5 ounces of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) a day was linked to a higher risk of chronic disease, according to a new large-scale analysis.

The study, published Sept. 22 in the journal Family Medicine and Community Health, looked at nearly 8.8 million adults who participated in studies across the Americas, Europe, Asia and Oceania, with follow-up periods ranging from two to 32 years.

For every additional 100 grams of UPFs consumed daily, researchers found an association with a 14% higher risk of cardiovascular events, a 4% higher risk of cancer, a 3% higher risk of death from any cause and a 2% higher risk of metabolic syndrome or diabetes, according to a news release.

5 ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS THAT MAY BE WORSE FOR YOUR HEALTH THAN YOU THINK, EXPERT SAYS

UPFs are typically packaged and convenient, made through extensive industrial processing and often packed with additives. They can include sugary drinks, processed meats, packaged snacks and candy. One hundred grams is about the size of a 3.5-ounce bag of corn chips, a small box of candy or a single-serve cup of mini cookies.

Ultra-processed foods can include sugary drinks, processed meats, packaged snacks and candy, according to the analysis. (iStock)

People with the highest intake of UPFs also had higher risks of digestive diseases, depression or anxiety, obesity, cancer and cardiovascular events than those with the lowest intake of the foods.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Given that UPF-related chronic diseases often cluster as multimorbidity, reducing consumption of UPFs and replacing them with minimally processed alternatives may be relevant for chronic disease prevention and primary care management," the researchers, led by Xiao Liu, a cardiologist at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital in China and a research fellow at Duke-NUS Medical School in Singapore, wrote.

"A diet built around whole, minimally processed foods is one of the best investments we can make in our long-term health."

These types of foods tend to crowd out healthier, nutrient-dense options, according to Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder of Kelly's Choice.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"It's not that you can never eat them again," Springer, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital. "It's the fact that we are not getting real foods — real foods like fruits, vegetables, beans, nuts, whole grains."

Researchers said ultra-processed foods can add up throughout the day through snacks, sugary drinks and convenience foods. (iStock)

Rather than focusing on taking foods away, Springer recommended adding protein and fiber to meals and snacks. She suggested options such as an apple with peanut butter, nuts with cucumbers, or meals built around beans, chicken or tuna alongside fruits, vegetables and whole grains.

"A diet built around whole, minimally processed foods is one of the best investments we can make in our long-term health," she added.

Springer noted that the study was observational, so it cannot establish that UPFs directly caused the poor health outcomes.

It also relied on participants' self-reported diets and may not be able to account for other lifestyle factors.

A dietitian recommends emphasizing fruits, vegetables, whole grains and other minimally processed foods. (iStock)

Nonetheless, the study can teach people about the link between ultra-processed foods and chronic disease, Springer said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: 'Home Improvement' star Jonathan Taylor Thomas arrested for alleged public intoxication, resisting deputy
excerpt:
"Home Improvement" actor Richard Karn tells Fox News Digital his dad’s reaction to co-star and Playboy model Pamela Anderson joining the show.

body_text:
"Home Improvement" actor Richard Karn tells Fox News Digital his dad’s reaction to co-star and Playboy model Pamela Anderson joining the show.

"Home Improvement" star Jonathan Taylor Thomas was detained after reportedly resisting an officer in Westlake Village, CA on Monday.

According to court records obtained by Fox News Digital, Thomas was detained at the Malibu/Lost Hills sheriff's station. After being booked, Thomas was released shortly after.

Law enforcement sources told TMZ that the child actor was a passenger in a vehicle that was stopped by police. The outlet reported that deputies told Thomas to stay inside the vehicle, but he allegedly exited anyway. Thomas was also reportedly drunk at the time of the incident.

Law enforcement told People magazine: "The driver was being detained for DUI investigation. Sometime during the investigation, Mr. Taylor decided he would exit the vehicle. Deputies told him to sit back down in the vehicle. He was uncooperative with them, failed to follow orders, and obstructed the investigation, so he was arrested for obstruction, and he was arrested for drunk in public."

Jonathan Taylor Thomas, a child star in "Home Improvement," was reportedly detained for resisting an officer in California on Monday. (Getty Images)

Thomas's legal run in came shortly after he reunited with his "Home Improvement" co-stars Patricia Richardson and Taran Noah Smith.

‘HOME IMPROVEMENT’ STAR JONATHAN TAYLOR THOMAS MAKES RARE APPEARANCE IN REUNION PHOTO WITH CO-STARS

In August, Richardson sparked a wave of nostalgia when she shared a rare reunion photo with her former "Home Improvement" sons Thomas and Smith, more than 25 years after the beloved sitcom ended.

Zachery Ty Bryan, Taran Noah Smith and Jonathan Taylor-Thomas all starred in "Home Improvement." (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"My other boys," Richardson captioned the snapshot with a heart emoji.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Patricia Richardson shared a reunion photo with Taran Noah Smith and Jonathan Taylor Thomas. (Patricia Richardson/Instagram)

For eight seasons of the hit comedy series, Richardson played Jill Taylor, the wife of Tim Allen's character, Tim "The Toolman" Taylor. Thomas and Smith became household names, playing sons Randy and Mark Taylor, respectively, while Zachery Ty Bryan portrayed oldest son Brad.

The reunion offered fans a rare glimpse of Thomas, who largely stepped away from Hollywood after becoming one of the biggest child stars of the 1990s.

The "Home Improvement" cast included Zachery Ty Bryan, Tim Allen, Patricia Richardson, Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Taran Noah Smith, Richard Karn, Debbe Dunning and Earl Hindman. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Thomas rose to fame as Randy Taylor on "Home Improvement" and became a major teen heartthrob, appearing in films including "Tom and Huck" and "Man of the House." He also voiced young Simba in Disney’s 1994 blockbuster "The Lion King."

But at the height of his fame, Thomas made a surprising decision to walk away.

"I'd been going nonstop since I was 8 years old," Thomas told People in 2013. "I wanted to go to school, to travel and have a bit of a break."

Jonathan Taylor Thomas attended the WB Network's 2003 Winter Party. (Getty Images)

Thomas left "Home Improvement" during its eighth and final season, with his character moving to Costa Rica.

Although he largely stayed out of the spotlight, Thomas briefly returned to acting, reuniting with TV dad Tim Allen on "Last Man Standing" from 2013 to 2015. He appeared in four episodes and directed three.

Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur and quarterback Jacoby Brissett speak with the media following Arizona's 31-7 loss to the Seattle Seahawks.

The Arizona Cardinals’ season-opening victory over the Los Angeles Chargers was quickly overshadowed in Week 2, when they fell 31-7 to the defending champion Seattle Seahawks in Week 2.

Much of the postgame conversation centered on wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., who finished without a catch as Arizona’s offense struggled to find a rhythm. Last Sunday’s performance was the latest sign of a relatively quiet start to the 2026 season for the third-year receiver and No. 4 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft.

Harrison entered the league widely regarded as one of the top receiving prospects in recent memory, but he has managed just one reception for 33 yards through two games. He has yet to establish himself as a consistent part of the Cardinals’ passing game.

Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. (18) runs a route against the Los Angeles Chargers during the second half of an NFL game at SoFi Stadium on Sept. 13, 2026, in Inglewood, Calif. (Cooper Neill/Getty Images)

The concerns about Harrison’s development are not new. Injury setbacks limited him to 12 games last season, when he finished with 604 receiving yards and four touchdowns. The former Ohio State standout is still searching for his first 1,000-yard NFL season, and his slow start this year has only amplified the criticism surrounding him.

2026 NFL OROY ODDS: LOVE FAVORED; BOSTON RISES AFTER BIG WEEK 2

Harrison’s tape has shown flashes of the precise route running and polished technique that helped establish him as largely a "can’t-miss" prospect. At other times, however, he has appeared frustrated while dealing with drops or falling short of his own standards.

THREE WORD GAME: THREE WORDS TO DESCRIBE EVERY NFL TEAM SO FAR THIS SEASON AHEAD OF WEEK 3

Even as Harrison has struggled to find his footing, other players in Arizona’s offense have flourished. Tight end Trey McBride earned first-team All-Pro honors last season and emerged as one of the top players at his position. "I know it’s just ‘get some easy completions and get going,’" the first-year Cardinals coach noted. "You also have Trey McBride, who’s one of the best underneath guys in the world and there’s only about 60 to 65 plays a game. And you’ve got to run the ball. You’ve got Kendrick [Bourne], who works underneath pretty well, too. Everyone’s kind of got their role right there."

title: OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website, PM says
excerpt:
Albanese said it took "too long" for OpenAI to inform Australian officials of the breach in June

An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in...
body_text:
Albanese said it took "too long" for OpenAI to inform Australian officials of the breach in June

An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said.

The agent hacked a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time.

He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for taking "too long" to tell them about the breach, believed to be one of the world's first publicly reported AI-led hacks of a government website.

OpenAI said it only became aware of the incident in August "during an ongoing review" of "misaligned model activity", and told Australian officials on 10 September.

While the review is ongoing, a spokesperson for the AI firm said that it is not believed that any patient records were accessed.

Albanese said the breach occurred in June this year, but OpenAI only informed government officials via email on 10 September.

The prime minister said he had also expressed "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" when he spoke to Altman and there will "obviously be legal consequences on it".

Albanese said the agent accessed both public and non-public files and a "forensic investigation" is under way to find out if other government systems were affected.

The investigation will be led by the Australian Signals Directorate, the country's cybersecurity agency.

The public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal is administered by Services Australia, the main hub to redirect users to government services.

He told reporters: "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable."

Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.

title: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
excerpt:
Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new word

Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch ...
body_text:
Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new word

Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.

Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".

European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.

"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".

"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.

Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".

Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.

The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.

Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls"

Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.

But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.

Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.

However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.

Language around birth should be less judgemental

The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".

Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.

When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame.

"Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.

Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.

Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.

The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.

The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once.

"With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.

Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".

Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word

In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".

She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."

The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."

Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first.

"Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"

New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.

Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.

One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue.

"Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.

Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected.

"Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."

In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.

But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress.

"I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."
